In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices. Notably, the maximum feasible sum-rate value available with LASSO-based methods is essentially independent of other parameters, such as the number of devices or the number of active devices. Furthermore, the paper outlines a novel algorithm, dubbed grouper, which efficiently solves a relaxed version of the problem. To address issues related to group sizes, the paper suggests two solutions. Firstly, the approach of penalizing group sizes is explored. Secondly, the method of distributing the penalties according to the sizes of groups is presented. In both cases, the problem is reformulated as a reformulated grouper algorithm. Consistency and convexity of these reformulated algorithms are demonstrated. A comprehensive numerical analysis is conducted to evaluate the performance of these reformulated algorithms in comparison to existing solutions. A significant improvement in the maximum attainable sum-rate value, amounting to 30 percent, is observed with only a slight increase in the computational time required. A practical implementation of the proposed method is also considered, which involves a rounding operation to select groups. In this context, the method of distributing the penalties according to the sizes of groups is found to be more effective, resulting in a higher average sum-rate value, along with reduced interference at inactive user devices. A possible extension of the method to account for channel uncertainty is also explored. A simple multi-stage algorithm is presented to solve this more complex optimization problem. A comprehensive numerical analysis confirms the feasibility and efficacy of this approach. A significant improvement in the performance, measured by the average sum-rate value, is observed when using unstructured precoding in comparison to jointly selecting users and precoding with good performance, but a 30 percent gain is achieved when using the proposed method in the case of group precoding. A possible extension of the method to account for channel uncertainty, noise, and non-linear distortion is also considered. In this context, the method of jointly selecting users and precoding with group precoding demonstrates the best performance, resulting in the highest average sum-rate value, along with the lowest required outage probability, compared to all other possible precoding schemes, including unstructured precoding and two variants of group precoding.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a set of functions invariant under the mappings, and these functions can be generated by a given finite set. Ultimately, this results in a semimodular decomposition of the lattice consisting of divisors on a tropical curve, and this is achieved by applying a balanced metric on the curve's components such that the curve's divisor classes are determined by functions that satisfy the balanced metric condition. Ultimately, this results in a characterization of the curve's effective divisor classes. Moreover, for any tropical curve with a separation boundary, a specific divisor is identified such that the divisor's operations with any divisor that does not exceed the curve's boundary in terms of volume are effective. This effect is proven to be equivalent to the divisor being a multiple of a cycle that, when expressed in terms of a specific representation, has coefficients that do not exceed one. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary variants - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants collaborating with similar datasets, while in the latter, entities collaborate with diverse datasets that are composed of the same classes. Our key research objective is to design an optimal FL protocol that ensures privacy preservation and maximizes the model's performance in both scenarios. To this end, we develop a novel PLP protocol - an innovative approach that integrates private learning and partitioning - which aims to improve the efficiency of horizontal FL by applying a two-stage partitioning method. Initially, the model is partitioned into segments based on predicted class labels, followed by a refined partitioning process based on specific model parameters. This division enables participants to conceal their data from classes of less probability and share the rest with the server, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the joint model. Furthermore, we propose a novel vertical FL protocol called GVPLP, which involves an adaptive length determination method for partitions and employs the PLP technique to enhance its performance. Both protocols ensure the confidentiality of participants' data and the integrity of shared information. Moreover, they leverage an optimistic mirroring strategy to counteract potential misbehavior in FL settings. Lastly, we evaluate the efficiency of the PLP and GVPLP protocols in terms of their performance, scalability, and robustness through comprehensive experimentation. Interestingly, our findings reveal that PLP and GVPLP possess comparable efficiency, yet significantly outperform other competing protocols in both horizontal and vertical settings. Additionally, our protocols show great resilience against data corruption and various types of malicious behavior. Ultimately, our work contributes towards developing an innovative and powerful FL framework for multiple entities in a variety of machine learning scenarios and applications.

In a Smart City environment with numerous agencies and interconnected cyber and social layers, safeguarding public safety is becoming increasingly complex. To address this challenge, this study develops a sophisticated mathematical model that simulates the interactions and resource allocations between agencies when faced with terrorist attacks on both physical and cyber-social targets. The proposed model, Smart City Defense Game, considers the interactions among three players: the terrorist, the government, and the people. Each player has limited resources and makes sequential decisions with the government acting first, followed by the terrorist, and then the people. The model incorporates various factors such as target importance, agent resources, and agent perception to calculate payoff functions for the government and the people. The study shows that a sustainable Nash equilibrium exists and provides an explicit formula for calculating the Nash equilibrium values for the government and the people. Numerical simulations are conducted to analyze the impact of agent perception on the Nash equilibrium and the effectiveness of agents in preventing attacks. The results suggest that differences in agent perception lead to significantly varying Nash equilibrium values, and that under specific circumstances, agent perception influences attack outcomes with a large margin. The study also reveals scenarios where simultaneous attacks have lower costs than single attacks, indicating that combining attacks on different targets may be an advantageous strategy for the terrorist. Conversely, the government and the people may benefit from parallel attacks rather than a single assault. This research provides valuable insights into the complex relationships among agencies in maintaining Smart City public safety. The proposed model can be adapted to explore more agency-specific scenarios, such as two-government models to compare responses to attacks directed at physical and cyber-social targets. Additionally, variations of the model can be applied to conventional cities to distinguish agency behaviors based on public or terrorist characteristics. The study's findings may influence policy decisions and guide research into more nuanced agent behaviors within agency structures. The proposed models present an innovative approach to integrating mathematical modeling and simulation with machine learning to simplify complex agency interactions. Although the models focus solely on resource allocations and attacks, they reveal the intricate dynamics among agencies when multitasking and coordinating to counter attacks. The study highlights challenges in preventing large-scale attacks on multiple targets and emphasizes that agencies may face difficulties in stopping simultaneous attacks on various targets. A proposed algorithm demonstrates that simultaneous attacks may have benefits if the targets are not prioritized differently. Finally, the results indicate that agency coordination and information sharing can significantly counter attacks but also show that a lack of prioritization may lead to lower costs for the government and the people in certain scenarios. These outcomes encourage further research into more realistic agency characteristics, such as varying agent sizes

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a multi-agent control approach, combining local information from close-range vehicles and global information from the lead vehicle. Two distinct information networks are employed: a local, ring-shaped network and a global, line-shaped network. The control strategy is designed such that the distance between vehicles is maintained within predetermined limits, and the convergence of agent positions towards a targeted alignment is ensured, with convergence also occurring for vehicles within the final alignment. Critical parameters like the control response rate, the degree of responsiveness, and the relative importance of the global control are mathematically analyzed to confirm their impact on the system's behavior. Moreover, the research reveals that the system reaches a stable state and demonstrates that this stability point can be precisely controlled by adjusting the corresponding parameter. Ultimately, the study verifies its findings through simulation experiments, involving various scenarios with the vehicle positions, as well. The multi-agent control approach and its design offer significant practical contributions to the field of vehicle platooning, as they do not necessitate communication between vehicles, rely solely on real-time state information, and maintain a predictable and resilient control structure. The resulting design also exhibits characteristics like sparseness, locality, differentiability, and continuousness, which provides substantial practical advantages. Additionally, the research provides a comprehensive understanding of the parameter design for the multi-agent control approach. The study's results remain unaffected by the system's uncertainties, and it ultimately offers a control strategy suitable for the challenging task of vehicle platooning over arbitrary paths. As future areas of research, the study suggests exploring novel strategies for paths that are not in the final alignment and examining the feasibility of the multi-agent control approach for the related task of vehicle trajectory following. The study's preliminary findings indicate that the key technical difficulties can be overcome, opening up the possibility for further in-depth investigations, which would significantly advance the field of multi-agent control. The study's initial exploration of the related task identified the potential for developing a control strategy, which could be extended by conducting more in-depth analyses, particularly in the examination of the multi-agent control approach for the task of vehicle trajectory following. The study's preliminary findings have revealed that the key technical difficulties can be overcome, offering a basis for further investigations, which would substantially contribute to the field of multi-agent control. The research suggests that the related task of vehicle trajectory following is an appropriate area for further examination, as it is a more intricate and demanding control challenge, which could be effectively addressed through the proposed control approach

One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our proposed technique, Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD), avoids requiring communication during iterations by simultaneously computing gradients from numerous data samples before exchanging the final gradient values at a designated frequency, allowing for a substantial reduction in communication overhead. This technique is extensively analyzed and numerically demonstrated to yield superior results when compared to traditional SGD in various scenarios, including non-convex optimization, which includes training Inception and ResNet models, and quadratic programs, which includes regression on the CIFAR10 dataset. The source code for our technique is available at https://github.com/parietz/communication-avoiding-sgd under the MIT license. This study showcases that, for sufficiently large enough aggregation frequencies, CA-SGD converges to equivalent fixed points as SGD. Additionally, our research explores and analyzes the performance of CA-SGD in terms of its communication complexity and reveals that its communication overhead can be made arbitrarily small within a polynomial time complexity by extending the aggregation frequency technique. This extension is theoretically validated to converge to equivalent fixed points as SGD. Finally, our numerical experiments confirm the existence of an optimal aggregation frequency, varying based on the specific problem at hand, that minimizes communication overhead while accelerating convergence. An additional benefit of our technique is that it enables simultaneous aggregation of gradients from multiple layers, increasing its communication efficiency by up to 43.33% and speeding up its convergence by as much as 85.57%. For instance, using our technique to train an Inception model on the ImageNet dataset at the aggregation frequency of 1024 results in a substantial time savings of around 39.3 days when compared to training the model using a batch size of 1024 over the entire dataset. Consequently, this time savings allows for a substantial increase in the achievable inference latency of Google Cloud AI Platform for training the model. In particular, training the model over Google Cloud AI Platform for virtual machines type n1-standard-8 yields an achievable inference latency of 335 ms, corresponding to the time required for the last layer to complete. By optimizing the technique to distribute computational tasks among available hardware components, our technique achieves an accelerated convergence that is up to 5.16 times faster than SGD, while also resulting in a substantial communication overhead reduction of up to 43.33

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. For a long time, detecting deepfakes focused solely on visual evidence, but as machine learning capabilities improve, systems can now create realistic audio components as well. However, identifying false information becomes increasingly difficult when the falsification is minimal and specifically designed to confuse an individual. A new study demonstrates an efficient method of enhancing the accuracy of fact-checking for computer-generated headlines by categorizing texts into human-generated and computer-generated passages simultaneously. Analyzing the distribution of words help separate human-generated text from computer-generated text, but since each has a unique set of characteristics, word distributions are not effective for classification. Therefore, a model based on bidirectional transformers was utilized for classification purposes. The study involved gathering a substantial dataset consisting of 3 million human-generated and 1 million computer-generated headlines and found that the transformer model outperformed leading propagation-based and convolutional neural network models, with an accuracy rate of 95.09% and a recall rate of 93.95%. The proposed method offers an affordable and efficient technique without the need for specialized hardware such as GPUs. The study's findings can contribute to the development of an automatic fact-checking system for multimedia content by supplementing traditional signal-based verification with language-based validation in mismatch detection. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, but its results are valid only when input data from all antennas are simultaneously available. This leads to the necessity of pre-processing data from individual moving antennas before the cross-correlation, thus eliminating time synchornization benefits. A more promising solution, known as the direct-correlator architecture, yields accurate results without the need for pre-processing, though it lacks the computational benefits of the FFT-correlator. By combining the concepts from both methods, a novel FFT-direct correlator is proposed, leveraging the computational efficiency of the FFT-correlator while providing accurate results without additional data processing. The proposed FFT-direct correlator architecture reduces computational complexity compared to the traditional architecture, making it particularly suitable for large-scale arrays, where it could significantly reduce computational overhead by factors of 20-40. Real-world applications in fields like finance, geography, and medicine require discovering
causal relationships between a dataset and a target variable. To address this, we propose a novel
method for identifying correlation between a conditional generative model's parameters and the target

indicates a positive correlation with the target variable, while a poor generator indicates a 
negative correlation. The proposed CPGP method sorts the generated samples from different models 
based on their similarity to real data, then uses a parameter optimization technique to find the optimal 
generator. To measure the correlation between the parameters of a conditional generative model 
and the target variable, we employ a similarity metric between data distributions. The results 
show that our CPGP method successfully detects the known directional relationship between the S&P 500 
index and Gold price, as well as other, less obvious correlations, such as the positive relationship 
between the prices of Copper and Gold. The source code for our real-world application can be found

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying a diverse set of 53 users and collecting their feedback on a 
range of solutions, which included translating content, making content more 
visually appealing, and using special effects. Our analysis of the feedback 
revealed that users prioritize clear and appealing visual content over translation 
or effects, but this preference comes with technical limitations in implementing 
translations and effects. Our study's implications have implications for creators and 
developers, suggesting that users value content that is both clear and 
attractive. Our code and dataset are publicly available for further research. 

Significant social networking disparities can result in users feeling left out and 
unengaged, partly due to a lack of accessible user-generated content. While 
available solutions, such as translation and effects, aim to reduce this disparity, 
the user perspective on these options remains largely unknown. To gain a deeper 
understanding, our research investigated how users can participate in creating and 
sharing content using new forms of media, like images, videos, and GIFs. A total of 
53 users took part in our study, providing valuable insights that highlighted 
particular challenges and trade-offs associated with using these solutions. 

Our research involved presenting participants with various content examples that 
demonstrated their preference for clear and appealing visual content across all 
media types, yet faced practical limitations in implementing translations and effects 
- although this was more common for users generating content using special effects. 
Notably, users favor content that is both clear and appealing but may compromise 
on this preference if it results in slower loading times. 

Our research suggests that users value content that is both clear and appealing, but 
may prioritize accessibility over content quality. This preference is consistent 
across all media types. 

Our research implies that creators and developers should prioritize user perspectives 
when designing accessible social networking solutions, taking into account users' 
trade-offs and limitations when creating and sharing content across various media 
types.

Building on Church encodings in typed lambda-calculi, we plan to develop a new
framework based on automata theory, which we call Church Automata Theory. This
framework is based on the concept of polyregular functions, a group of fast-
growth function classes derived from undecidable but fast-growing sets of
functions. We will use a specific coding system, analogous to Church encodings,
that utilizes finite automata instead of lambda-terms. This coding system will
allow us to represent transducers as codes similar to Church encodings. This
project aims to investigate the relationship between type systems and automata
theory, specifically how type checking can be interpreted as a constraint problem
on the associated regular functions, and finally apply this framework to study
complexity bounds of polyregular functions. This new framework offers an
original approach that combines type theory, coding theory, and automata theory. 

Key aspects of this proposal include:

- Establishing a comprehensive overview of polyregular functions, covering
key results from recent literature, including code schemes, such as Bowers' code,
and significant properties of polyregular functions.
- Introducing a specific lambda-calculus, based on a concept by Berardi, for
organizing these codes in a purely functional way, and analyzing their structural
properties. This will involve revisiting type systems with high computational
capabilities, such as Dybala's, for interpreting the fast-growing encodings.
- Defining a new model of automata theory, distinct from traditional notions,
that allows for a concise definition of polyregular functions and transducers.
This will involve modifying the notion of acceptance, specifically using
orthodox acceptance rather than acceptance by empty space.
 - Developing an innovative method to represent transducers as codes operating
on these modified automata, and establishing a central theorem linking type
checking to the consistency of these codes. This will involve translating the
growth rate of polyregular functions into regular functions' closure properties
under composition. Finally, we will derive new complexity bounds for polyregular
functions, building on established bounds in recent literature. This research
will offer fresh insights into the complexity of various classes of transducers.
It will also enable a systematic exploration of the relationship between type systems
and computational complexity, with a particular emphasis on polyregular functions. 
Additionally, our findings on the encoding of polyregular functions will have
positive consequences for other function classes where encodings based on
regular functions are used, such as the fast-growing Grigorev code.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. The current leading models, such as FastSQL, struggle when dealing with target databases that are similar to but distinct from the training databases. They tend to fill values inaccurately and overlook relevant database tables. To overcome these issues, we propose a training method that uses synthetic database shifts, called DBShifts. DBShifts optimizes database shifts during training by balancing value and schema transformations. Furthermore, we suggest a training method known as SynQ, which enhances data synthesis by mixing two types of datasets: one with detailed values and the other with comprehensive database information. The combination of SynQ and DBShifts significantly improves the leading models' performance, resulting in a record-breaking 87.3/82.3 on SPARTA's evaluation benchamark. By using sampled distributional parameters from historical data, our approach yields a robust, sample-based representation that effectively accounts for uncertainty, resulting in a more life-like model that captures probability distributions of states and velocities. By integrating our distributionally robust CVaR-based controller into navigation, we demonstrate its ability to withstand adverse outcomes and demonstrate up to 30% better performance compared to existing methods using traditional statistics. Furthermore, our method exhibits comparable efficiency in computational resources required. Experimental outcomes also reveal that our distributionally robust CVaR-based controller is more resilient to rare but high-impact events compared to other methods. By automating the process of data collection and policy design through AI, our method provides a more practical solution for real-world application. With its versatility, our distributionally robust CVaR-based method can be extended to other complex tasks, such as autonomous driving. In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for low-latency grant-free uplink access. First, the initial GA finds a subsampling strategy to transform a unitary matrix into a closely-packed, uniform pattern. Subsequently, a second-stage GA is employed to conceal 'distortion-inducing' data within the matrix, ensuring even power distribution. This genetic algorithm-based method is shown to outperform current grant-free uplink access methods, including those using structured sequences, in terms of reducing access latency when supporting a large number of users. Moreover, the proposed solution is found to be scalable and suitable for applications requiring fast activation and low-overhead signaling. It also offers the advantage of being easily adaptable to various, complex channel scenarios. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed genetic algorithm-based method achieves a significant reduction in both the number of symbols needed for sequence length determination and average pilot sequence length, resulting in a substantial latency improvement of multiple orders of magnitude. This research showcases the potential of genetic algorithms as a reliable tool for solving complex, high-dimensional optimization problems, particularly in next-generation wireless communications systems. The proposed genetic algorithm-based method is suggested as a viable solution for sequence generation in various grant-free uplink access scenarios, including those with high numbers of active users, emerging standards such as 5G-Nur, and 6G-related topics. Furthermore, this research is seen as a starting point for exploring the use of bio-inspired optimization algorithms in mMTC applications. Finally, the proposed solution is seen as a viable means of achieving low-latency communication systems in applications where high reliability is not a necessity, such as mMTC and mM-URLLC, to provide efficient and reliable communication. System designers can utilize this approach as a tool to determine whether bio-inspired optimization algorithms can solve complex, high-dimensional optimization problems effectively. A possible future research direction is to investigate the idea that standardization of sequence generation, which involves using specific algorithms, is suitable for large-scale deployments to provide reliable and efficient communication. A new strategy has emerged that aims to eliminate these inconsistencies by leveraging thermodynamic potentials derived from their natural variables. In this paper, this strategy is applied to both exact thermodynamic descriptions of moist air and two widely utilized simplifications: the fixed $\kappa$ approximation and the approximation based on dry heat capacities. Notably, a consistent $\kappa$ approximation yields a novel dynamical representation that relies solely on total mass and not on water forms when expressed using virtual potential temperature $\theta_v$. Furthermore, a vast compilation of thermodynamic concepts from multiple literature sources has been synthesized. It is the aspiration of this paper that it will serve as an authoritative reference for applying thermodynamic potentials in modeling moist thermodynamics. A comprehensive supplement detailing the derived thermodynamic equations is also provided. By highlighting the numerous assumptions underlying simplifications like the $\kappa$ approximation, this approach encourages critical evaluation of these assumptions and fosters exploration of when the approximations are valid, as well as the areas in between. Additionally, a tentative framework has been developed to generate thermodynamic descriptions based on machine learning techniques. By emphasizing that many simplifications are not invalid but rather valid approximations, this approach seeks to remove stigma associated with approximations, which in turn fosters a valid and efficient scientific strategy: if approximations are valid, they are suitable for modeling; if approximations are invalid, they likely generate incorrect results; if an description is a simplification, it likely produces less accurate outcomes; if descriptions are not a simplification, they likely fail to capture essential physical processes. Research on spoken dialogue systems has typically relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses for interpreting meaning and monitoring the dialogue flow.  Nevertheless, confusion networks (a more complex set of possible outcomes than a shortlist) can be a more natural choice.  This study explores the benefits of using confusion networks with a large number of possibilities (beyond the limited top ASR hypotheses) for interpreting and analyzing spoken dialogue inputs.  Firstly, confusion networks for a complete sentence transcript exhibit higher dimensional capacity than a shortlist, offering a more natural representation.  Secondly, using confusion networks for a single utterance - with a limited number of possible interpretations having specific confidence levels - is a more accurate model of human language interpretation.  Thirdly, we suggest incorporating confusion networks into statistical models for automatic speech recognition, integrating factors such as syntax and semantics into the likelihood function for a more comprehensive analysis.  This approach is a more natural representation, allowing for a more in-depth analysis of language.  Finally, we examine the potential of using confusion networks for analyzing and understanding spoken dialogue data, beginning with an analysis of utterance-level networks and proposing methods for measuring uncertainty regarding an utterance's semantics.  This could ultimately pave the way for a more in-depth analysis of dialogue analysis.  This work is currently in progress and results will be presented at the workshop. In this study, a different strategy is explored where a pre-trained model is fixed and only the predictions of the predictions layer are updated during subsequent tasks. This simplified, parameter-efficient strategy is evaluated using widely recognized benchmarks such as CIFAR30, CIFAR100, and ImageNet-1K, and the results demonstrate that freezing the pre-trained model and updating the predictions is an effective way to continual learning without complex modifications or increasing model complexity. The code for this study is available online at the specified repository link. The outcomes reveal that updating only the predictions results in a near-similar performance when compared to updating the entire predictions layer with an optimizer, while updating the predictions consistently outperforms updating the last layer separately for each task. In a comparative evaluation with respect to widely recognized CL methods, updating the predictions successfully resolves the problem of catastrophic forgetting over 75% of the time, and the results show that updating the predictions is an efficient and straightforward way to continual learning. The study also examines the theoretical underpinnings of updating the predictions and identifies areas for further research in understanding this parameter-efficient strategy for continual learning. As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and contextual nuances. Furthermore, few attempts have been made to explore the explainability of such models, given the severe social and legal repercussions of inaccurate predictions. Our research introduces a sophisticated, deep learning-based framework that integrates multimodal inputs: (a) to accurately recognize hate speech by grasping the text's underlying meaning and its social and cultural context, and (b) to provide actionable insights into our model's decision-making processes. Our extensive evaluation showcases that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art hate speech classification techniques, emphasizing the significance of social and cultural context features in uncovering hate-related categories. Additionally, our model yields more transparent and explainable outcomes compared to other deep learning-based hate speech classification methods. Our research performs a thorough analysis of the elements that influence our model's accuracy, thereby increasing user trust in our system. Our ultimate goal is to develop a practical, user-centric system that leverages AI-powered hate speech detection and explanation to combat this global issue. This system will enable various stakeholders, such as platform moderators, social organizations, and individual users, to tackle hate speech more effectively, by utilizing our model for prediction and explanation. We also intend to share our research outcomes and collaborate with social organizations to implement our model in real-world settings. We conducted a pilot study with two social organizations, providing them with access to our model's prediction and explanation capabilities. We observed that they were particularly interested in our model's explainability, as it allowed them to gain a deeper understanding of the context in which hate speech emerges. This, in turn, facilitated their efforts to create customized intervention strategies aimed at preventing hate speech. Conversely, we discovered that professionals were primarily concerned with the accuracy of our model predictions. Upon achieving state-of-the-art performance and explainability, our model successfully addressed an array of research questions related to hate speech classification and detection. Ultimately, our hope is that our research contributes meaningfully to the ongoing discussions surrounding the complex issue of hate speech and highlights the significance of AI-powered hate speech explanation in combating this global problem. We are confident that our future research will shed further light on hate-related topics and, ultimately, aid in the reduction of hate speech on social media platforms. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that broader in-degree distribution widths eliminate oscillations, whereas a broader out-degree distribution width may induce oscillations in synaptically coupled networks. Additionally, we observe that gap junction coupling weakly impacts network dynamics. These results are highly relevant to inhomogeneous cortical networks, where in-degree distribution widths can significantly impact oscillations. Furthermore, our research explores the effects of heterogeneity in out-degree distribution widths and investigates the emergence of collective oscillations in networks of theta neurons. Through stochastic resonance analysis, we demonstrate that these networks are capable of efficiently detecting weak signals, with the out-degree distribution playing a crucial role in this process. We have developed a novel, transport-based approach for determining the Equation-of-State of nuclear matter from high-energy collider experiments. By simulating mid-central proton-proton and proton-lead collisions using a dynamic Monte Carlo model, we analyze both the transverse momentum distribution and multivariate cumulants of secondary particles. Our findings show that the Equation-of-State is characterized by the nuclear shear viscosity over entropy ratio and specific entropy at equilibrium. We demonstrate that the flow coefficients of secondary particles are sensitive to both parameters but also heavily influenced by initial state conditions. However, when assuming a pre-defined value for the nuclear shear viscosity, we are able to constrain the Equation-of-State by simulating nuclear collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Our results suggest a weak increase in entropy for dense nuclear matter as the energy density rises, but a significant gap remains for determining the exact nature of this behavior. Furthermore, we show that our method provides a plausible explanation for measured di-hadron cumulant anomalies. To confidently determine the Equation-of-State, we show that future experiments should be designed such that the initial state conditions have minimal influence on measured cumulant anomalies. The method developed here can be extended to study other critical properties of hot and dense nuclear matter. Furthermore, we show that our method can be applied to study similar multivariate phenomena at lower energies by comparing to Monte Carlo models that simulate quark-gluon plasma formation. Ultimately, with continued experimental improvement and a deeper understanding, we anticipate the Equation-of-State of nuclear matter to be precisely determined. The approach outlined here presents an essential step in achieving that goal. A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in various wireless communication systems, focusing on a binary classification model. We evaluate GNN performance in both unencoded and encoded systems, then propose innovative retransmission techniques to address data transmission errors and improve GNN prediction accuracy. Our research involves simulation-based validation on synthetic graph data, demonstrating the effectiveness of our retransmission mechanisms and providing valuable insights for practical applications. The results show that using our retransmission techniques yields significantly higher GNN prediction rates compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we analyzed the communication efficiency of our retransmission methods and found that model-driven retransmission techniques outperform their counterparts. Ultimately, our retransmission techniques offer promising solutions for enhancing GNN performance in various practical scenarios. We focus on a convex function $f$, which has properties $\alpha \geq \alpha_m > 0$, and is strongly-convex with parameter $\alpha$. We use SGD with step sizes that decrease exponentially, which still allows us to achieve a faster convergence rate. We modify the classic SGD algorithm by adding an adaptive correction term, which is designed to counter 'inner' variability in the function, while adjusting for its covariance. This correction is optimized using a reduced set of past data. Combining this with the modified SGD, we obtain an adaptive algorithm that is robust to the changing conditions of the function. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we develop DistillIdentity, a dedicated loss function for pristine layer representations, and introduce DistillActivation, which enables value-based distillation for pruned layers. Through these enhancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving notable reductions in parameters and computational requirements while maintaining competitive accuracy on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-10. Our accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alefilfan/Indentify. This version of the code has been updated to reflect corrections mentioned in the paper's Appendix C. Specifically, the revised code removes the model compression application step and related utilities, as the specified compression method (IndDistill itself) is inherently implemented within the Pytorch framework (v1.9.0 and later). Consequently, our example usage demonstration only includes the distillation of the student network from the teacher network, with the knowledge transfer parameters being set directly. While the original paper's results were generated using Pytorch v1.8.1, the revised code is compatible with the latest Pytorch version. Lastly, our dedicated neural architecture search framework, named ArchInd, can be accessed at https://github.com/alefilfan/ArchIdent. This framework enables the efficient discovery of scalable neural architectures by integrating principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning. Through ArchInd, we successfully identified the scalable ResNet50-L L0.5 model, which boasts 25 million parameters and an top-1 accuracy of 93.44% on the ImageNet dataset, surpassing the conventional knowledge-based designs (e.g. ResNet50) and current state-of-the-art model compression approaches (e.g. EfficientNet). Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this relationship is not always valid; however, we define a specific class of linear-like functions with sufficient complexity and provide criteria under which the converse is true, establishing a definitive topological invariant for this particular subset of linear-like functions. Additionally, we identify a subset of linear-like functions where the converse is false even when they are locally homeomorphic. The criteria we established also reveals that the topological conjugacy of linear-like functions is not solely determined by the orbit of a single point, as previously established for hyperbolic functions. Furthermore, we define a subset of quasi-linear functions with sufficient complexity and find that a topological conjugation between them can be extended to a hyperbolic bundle isomorphism for this particular subset of quasi-linear functions. Therefore, the concept of topological conjugacy is equivalent to the hyperbolic bundle isomorphism for this particular subset of quasi-linear functions.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria. Furthermore, several examples are provided to illustrate that these conditions are not merely less restrictive, but also significantly so. In addition, a conditional differentiability theorem is proven and is expressed as follows: a function with n real variables is differentiable under the condition that, for every point, there exists a sphere within which certain partial differentiability conditions are met. This conditional differentiability criterion is shown to be an extension of a previous result, which was established by Hamilton. Moreover, several significant outcomes derive from the differentiability conditions presented in this study. Firstly, a new necessary and sufficient condition for differentiating a function with two real variables is provided and is shown to be an extension of a previous result achieved by Dini. Additionally, a new conditional integrability criterion was discovered, which is an extension of an earlier result obtained by Birkhoff and Boron. Finally, a new sufficient condition for differentiating a function with n real variables was found, as well as a new conditional integrability criterion for functions with n real variables. Moreover, these conditions were shown to be an extension of several previous results, with full details provided in the context of this study. Lastly, it is worth noting that several significant problems remain open in this context, with full details presented in the final section of this work.

Our analysis revealed a significant correlation between the mass transported by outflows and the star formation rate density across various regions. Notably, we found that regions with the highest star formation rates have the highest outflow masses, although the outflow mass does not always surpass the star formation rate. By comparing the outflow mass to the star formation rate, we found that regions within 100 parsecs of each other have a higher negative correlation than regions apart from each other. Furthermore, we found that the outflow mass is primarily composed of gas with high velocities, indicating a link between the outflows and the most intense regions of star formation. The number of connected devices has seen tremendous growth, creating vast volumes of diverse data that intertwine with our physical world. The Edge Intelligence System has emerged to harness edge computing and AI, facilitating intelligent services through powerful processing and near-instant decision-making. With a central server orchestrating entire systems, existing frameworks still struggle with security risks, but they offer a crucial stepping stone for future Intelligent Transportation Systems, particularly within vehicle networks. To address existing concerns, a concept for secure edge intelligence is proposed, combining Federated Learning, blockchain technology, and Local Differential Privacy to improve accuracy and safety, enhance user privacy, and maintain data integrity through immutable, distributed ledger networks and secure reward systems. Local Differential Privacy takes it a step further, ensuring confidentiality of shared data while safeguarding private user data from malicious attacks. The proposed framework has been effectively tested in scenarios using synthetic data, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness against malicious behavior. The comprehensive framework presents a promising framework for reliable, scalable, and secure edge intelligence for future intelligent transportation systems. The source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/EdgarRendon/FEDLP. The research findings showcase the potential of edge intelligence with enhanced safety, privacy, and reliability for applications in intelligent transportation and beyond. The proposed framework presents a promising solution for the challenges in vehicle networks while opening doors for broader adoption across various use cases. The research contributes a novel, practical solution for secure edge intelligence with improved accuracy, privacy, and dependability. The proposed framework serves as an essential component for trustworthy AI systems within vehicle networks and can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks, including those based on IEEE 802.11u-2016 standards. The research and implementation provide valuable insights for developers and institutions to design and deploy secure edge intelligence for future intelligent transportation systems, showcasing the importance of trustworthy AI systems in vehicle networks. The research demonstrates a successful prototype, highlighting the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed solution in real-world applications. The synthesis of research as presented in this paper is eligible for automatic translation into the language specified in UNESCO's PLP. The research presented in this dissertation contributes theoretically and practically to the advancement of edge intelligence systems with enhanced security, privacy, reliability, and scalability. The proposed edge intelligence system effectively mitigates existing challenges in vehicle networks and the transportation sector, offering a valuable framework for designing and implementing trustworthy AI systems within vehicle networks. The research and implementation of the edge intelligence system with blockchain and FEDLP successfully address critical issues in the field, providing a reliable and trustworthy solution for intelligent transportation and beyond

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous applications, especially in dimension 2. While it lacks a straightforward multi-variable definition, this research introduces a circumvention to employ it in high-dimensional spaces. In particular, this characteristic is used to determine the topological differences between different data sets retrieved from the UCI Machine Learning Database. By combining the concept of sublevel sets with a form of symbolic topological data analysis known as Cech persistent homology, this study explores data analysis based on quantities instead of the traditional approach using distances. Utilizing computational software, the outcomes demonstrate how this method can distinguish various data sets, with discussions surrounding potential challenges and possibilities for improving data analysis. Additionally, this study discusses some theoretical difficulties regarding consistency that arise when applying topological data analysis techniques based on the Euler characteristic. It further suggests possible applications of this characterization in data analysis. Finally, this study outlines future research directions, including the extension of this method to utilize complete metric spaces and multi-variable spaces, as well as the exploration of other topological invariants for potential applications in data analysis. Several open questions are posed regarding multi-variable topological data analysis. Although characterized topological data analysis based on the Euler characteristic may not offer significant advantages over other characterized methods, it possesses several distinct advantages due to its simplicity. In particular, this study highlights how this method surpasses other characterized methods in several respects, including applicability, flexibility, and computational feasibility. While this study primarily focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces, it outlines characterized topological data analysis as a broader field, highlighting significant contributions, limitations, and open questions. Several characterized topological data analysis methods discussed in this study include those based on distances, symbolic topological data analysis, persistent homology, Cech homology, and complete metric spaces. In particular, this study explores data analysis based on quantities in multi-variable spaces, revisits topological data analysis in complete metric spaces, and examines multi-variable topological data analysis based on the second Euler characteristic. Furthermore, this study discusses characterized topological data analysis as a tool for advanced quantitative data analysis and discusses several open questions and challenges. Finally, this study outlines several potential future research directions related to topological data analysis methods and characters. Several applications of multi-variable topological data analysis based on the Euler characteristic are explored, with discussions extending to related fields, including topological data analysis

By saturating the prey population's ability to evade predation and the predator population's hunting efficiency, we modified the classic equations. Additionally, we incorporated an intraspecific competition factor into the prey population's growth rate, balancing the prey species' dynamics with the predator population's survival through predation. A stable equilibrium was found for the species coexistence, as well as predator-prey and disease-free pure species and prey-only equilibrium states. Furthermore, we determined the species' extinction points, describing the various dynamic transitions, and creating corresponding phase diagrams that illustrate the complex interplay between disease spread, species coexistence, and extinction. A thorough mathematical examination revealed the significant impact of parameter adjustments on equilibrium points, revealing the delicate balance among species' survival, disease spread, and species competition. The findings offer insights into ecosystems' dynamic evolution, allowing predictions of species' fates in naturally occurring systems. Building on a graded version of Quillen-Suslin theory, we establish an analogous concept for graded rings. Additionally, by integrating recent results from endomorphism rings of vector spaces over polynomial rings, we gain a thorough understanding of the k-torsion issue in these endomorphism rings. Consequently, this gives us a complete diagnosis of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R) for rings R = (R0, X_1,..., X_n). A significant particular case arises when R is a polynomial ring. All k-torsion elements in the resulting nil-groups are exactly the elements obtained through repeated multiplication by elements from the coefficients {X_1,..., x_n} and their inverses. Consequently, the k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R) becomes a part of the nil-class group, a concept proposed here, and is thus asymptotically nilpotent. This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques. We reveal the discrepancies between the full wave function generation approach and the CWFS method, with the latter incorporating the resonance approximation for the top quark propagator and treating it as a standard reference to evaluate the impact of these off-shell and non-resonant contributions. We find that off-shell/top resonance contributions are generally minor but may become significant in specific situations (e.g., high p_T l+ in tt-jet interactions). Non-resonant effects in general have a more substantial effect, particularly in kinematic regions where the resonance peak is expected to be minimal. Consequently, determining the correct forms of differential distributions in these scenarios will be essential for accurately extracting the top quark mass using the template fitting method. Furthermore, to facilitate this, we provide the UNESM code, which computes various differential distributions for the ttbar+jet processes in the channel of two leptons and one jet, both with and without the narrow width assumption, to allow for a better understanding of these off-shell and non-resonant influences. We also provide a UNESM interface to learn more about the differences between the full and CWFS approaches during the analysis. We are confident that the insights and distributions provided will enhance the precision of top quark mass determination via template fitting. We believe that our work will be of use to those engaged in direct and indirect determinations of the top quark mass and its associated uncertainties. We have written a document outlining the key steps required to generate various distributions for the process of pp -> ttj using the full propagator implementation, a description of the code, its components and tools, with detailed instructions on the setup, variables and distribution extraction. We are now prepared to address the task of determining the top quark mass via template fitting. We have begun by calculating the ratio of the full propagator distribution to the CWFS one, with the aim of reducing statistical uncertainty, a decision that will enable us to extract the impact of off-shell/top resonance effects in differential distributions. We have created the TtbarPropagator code, which generates these ratios for the (ttbar+jet) process in the channel of two leptons

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. Research into more robust and adaptable systems remains an active area, necessitating further investigation. In our study, we present a more efficient and versatile approach that outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both settings. Specifically, we use a novel attack detection approach that treats anti-spoofing as a multi-class problem, including the classification of legitimate faces, spoof attacks, and unknown entities. Our model leverages an iterative attention mechanism to selectively highlight relevant facial characteristics. By integrating Attention Transfer Layers (ATLs) into existing CNNs, we enable them to adapt to unfamiliar attack methods by transferring knowledge from a specialized anti-spoofing network. Our experiments demonstrate exceptional performance, with an average AUC of 99.76% across six datasets, a significant improvement over the previous best multi-domain average of 97.39%. Additionally, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art single-domain performance on the CASIA-Spoofing dataset. We also provide a simpler, parameter-efficient special case of our attack detection method, called Attention Validation Layer (AVL), which integrates seamlessly into existing networks. ATL and AVL are valuable new tools for the field of anti-spoofing research. Our source code is available for public access at https://github.com/jaykim21/AttentionTransferLayer. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, given its relevance due to autonomous driving's inherent complexities along with the challenges posed by environmental interactions and adaptive learning errors. In our framework, a longitudinal acceleration command serves as the optimal control strategy since it influences overall driving behavior while exhibiting dynamic characteristics that evolve based on vehicle mass, friction coefficient, and curve radius. Utilizing data generated by the OpenAI Gym-based Autonomous Driving Gym, we have successfully implemented a end-to-end deep reinforcement learning framework consisting of a Curvature-Based Lane Assist Network and a Motor Control Network. In doing so, we have tackled a challenging problem within deep reinforcement learning, namely the scarcity of available training sets. In order to resolve this issue, we have introduced the use of a curriculum learning strategy that divides the training set into distinct stages featuring an increasing level of curvature. In a simulated testing environment, our framework exhibited stable learning capabilities, including the ability to learn a robust curvature estimation model and an efficient motor control strategy. In particular, our findings demonstrate that our approach remains stable during the execution of curves having radii exceeding 50 meters at a speed of 50 mph, including situations in which the vehicle loses sight of the curve or encounters uncertainties in the friction coefficient. In conclusion, our work involves the first reported end-to-end deep reinforcement learning application for autonomous driving based on the OpenAI Gym Autonomous Driving Gym. In doing so, we have successfully resolved several challenging problems within the field, including the lack of available training sets, robust learning stability, and robust learning performance. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As APEAs provide a higher chance of selection to quicker solutions, the evaluation time bias negatively affects the overall search performance. Despite the significant impact of evaluation time bias on APEAs, there is a lack of comprehensive research investigating this phenomenon. Therefore, this study thoroughly examines the effects of evaluation time bias on the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms, with a particular focus on reducing its impact. Our research evaluates various strategies, including traditional approaches like parallel evaluation and population sizing, as well as more innovative methods, such as the effect cancellation technique and the efficiency equalization strategy. Our experiments demonstrate that integrating these methods effectively minimizes the evaluation time bias and enhances the efficiency of Asynchronous PEAs. With the effect cancellation strategy combined with the efficiency equalization, the APEAs exhibit population sizes that can be 43% larger than those without the bias, ultimately resulting in better-converged solutions in a reduced timeframe. These findings validate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches in mitigating the evaluation time bias problem of parallel evolutionary algorithms. With the promising results, it is anticipated that these methods will also benefit the performance of multi-objective optimization algorithms, as they often employ PEAs as the fundamental computing platform. Our research showcases the scalability of our methods by successfully testing them on various applications, such as traditional evolutionary strategies, as well as multi-objective optimization and hyperparameter tuning tasks. Our work provides a significant contribution to the optimization community, as our proposed methods not only rectify existing parallel evolutionary algorithm design flaws, but also open up avenues for further research into the decoupling of solution evaluations, a longstanding challenge in the field. As future directions, it is suggested that dynamic resource allocation based on task complexity could complement our methods, with the aim of further enhancing Asynchronous PEAs. Our research showcases the dynamic of solution quality distribution during the search process in various scenarios, with the goal of facilitating a deeper understanding of the interplay between complexity and scalability in parallel evolutionary algorithms. Additionally, our method of decoupling solution evaluations has the potential to contribute significantly to the advancement of multi-objective optimization and system design optimization by providing a fundamental computing platform. The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, applying this principle to many-body systems connected to baths poses significant challenges. Our research focuses on the behavior of periodically driven quantum open systems, revealing two distinct phases defined by the Floquet generator's nature - a chaotic, within the system's subspace eigenbasis ergodic phase and a regular phase, where dynamics are contained within an infinitely long-lived meta-stable state. We examine the system's thermodynamic properties in both phases and investigate the emergence of a nonequilibrium steady state after a driving period in the regular phase. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of environmental effects, like dephasing and fluctuation-induced effects, which couple the system to a bath. We establish that high-frequency expansions can fall short, and only approximately describe the Floquet generator's eigenvalues, necessitating an iterative correction to accurately determine them. Lastly, we obtain the Floquet APW method, describing the system's evolution on driving periods, and analyze the system-state population at the driving period's end. The results reveal a correlation between the system's occupation and the exponential decay rate of the wavepacket. Notably, in nearly integrable systems, this exponential decay is significantly slower and often much closer to the system's subspace eigenstate lifetime. The research provides new insights into open systems, uncovering novel phenomena and challenges that arise in isolated systems when extended to open quantum systems, and offers a potential solution to long-standing issues in open systems, such as the system's dissipation to thermal equilibrium. The study also offers a new method for analyzing eigenstates, capable of detecting hidden symmetries in the system. Ultimately, our analysis may lead to the discovery of novel phases and states that are not found in isolated systems but are present in open quantum systems subjected to high-frequency drives. The findings have far-reaching implications for understanding a broad range of phenomena in diverse fields such as solid-state physics, biology, and nonlinear dynamics. As future work, investigating the interplay between high-frequency drives and environmental effects, particularly dephasing and the system-bath coupling, could provide a deeper understanding of this complex problem. The study presents an entirely new and highly accurate method, iterative correction of Floquet Hamiltonian, which is also applicable to closed systems but yields far superior results in the context of open systems. It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these learned features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this paper, a new approach is presented that involves identifying an optimal set of features, rather than specifying the feature learning process in advance. By combining the benefits of deep feature transformers and shallow feature selectors, the proposed method facilitates better generalization to target datasets with distinct underlying features. Additionally, the computational requirements of the traditional iterative approach can be significantly reduced using an alternative training method. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed approach over traditional deep learning methods in various feature selection tasks. Furthermore, the proposed method's computational efficiency is comparable to existing alternatives, while its ability to extract relevant features allows it to outperform shallower selection-only networks. Experimental evaluations were conducted using a range of well-known classification datasets, including MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN. By applying the proposed method to these datasets, the results indicate that feature selection can be effectively utilized not only to reduce computational requirements but also to identify key features that contribute to network performance. The proposed method's code is publicly available on the GitHub platform at the URL https://github.com/JingwangGao/DeepFeatureSelect. Experimental evaluations conducted over multiple runs yielded consistent results, highlighting the proposed method's effectiveness in extracting relevant features from datasets. The proposed method's application to target datasets with distinct underlying characteristics resulted in a performance boost of up to 6.63%, along with computational cost reductions of approximately 81%. The experiments demonstrate that feature selection can be an efficient and effective approach in both feature selection tasks and classification tasks, by identifying prominent features that contribute significantly to network performance. The proposed method employs a transformer module consisting of a convolutional layer, a long short-term memory (LSTM) unit, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP), which facilitates better generalization to target datasets with distinct underlying characteristics. The convolutional layer tends to detect features with spatial relationships, the LSTM unit captures temporal features, and the MLP applies nonlinear mapping to improve the network's overall generalizability. The alternative training method reduces the proposed approach's training time by dividing the optimization process into smaller, more efficient iterations, rather than using an iterative approach that requires more computational resources and precision. The experiments conducted in this study provide valuable insights into the fields of deep feature selection, transformer optimization, and deep learning generalization, highlighting the proposed method's unique strengths and significant contributions.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but fail to account for the underlying general principles generated by the model. As a result, these methods cannot accurately predict predictions for novel, unseen instances. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel method called ProGNN, which involves creating a graph-procedure to accurately extract general principles (graph patterns and node features) generated by a GNN to support its predictive decisions. Our proposed approach empowers the identification of significant graph patterns that affect predictions, thus enhancing our ability to discover essential rules that can be generalized to novel cases. Experimental findings obtained from our implementation of ProGNN demonstrate its effectiveness in producing interpretable results for diverse types of GNNs, as well as its applicability to prediction tasks. Additionally, our results show that ProGNN can significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods used for the explanation of GNNs, thus further validating its worth. Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, a comprehensive understanding of the LMU is established by adapting the conceptual framework of the Transformer to analyze the RNN family, including the LMU. Key differences between the LMU and traditional RNN/Transformer models, such as the Long Short Term Memory network and the autoregressive transformer, are identified and assessed. Critical parameters, such as training loss and the distribution of weights within the LMU, were examined to elucidate the mechanism leading to the improved performance of the LMU. Additionally, the study reveals that the improvement achieved by the LMU can be attributed to the avoidance of a common bias during data training. Theoretical explanations and demonstrations are provided to illustrate potential noise introduction and performance degradation in the LMU. Furthermore, the study proposes a series of design enhancements aimed at further enhancing the capabilities of the LMU. By understanding the theoretical foundations of the LMU, developers are empowered to independently create and customize improved recurrent neural networks based on their specific needs. The source code for the LMU has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/pcullen/legendre-memory-unit. The study also highlights potential applications and further developments for the LMU in the existing literature. The study ultimately suggests that the performance gains of the LMU are limited and full potential may require the use of further data augmentation techniques. The study also finds while the LMU achieves better results than the Transformer on certain tasks, the choice of LMU activation is critical as it can lead to underperformance due to the choice of the Legendre polynomials basis. The study proposes a new method called the Diagonalization Activation Mechanism (DiAM) to address this issue, which achieves state-of-the-art performance and provides a more systematic approach to design better recurrent neural networks activation functions. The source code for the DiAM has been made publicly available at https://github.com/pcullen/diam. The study concludes by outlining the current challenges and potential next steps for the design of recurrent neural networks. As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's imbalance of matter over antimatter, the seemingly calculated balance of the electro-weak scale, and various fundamental physics aspects.  A significant new research frontier has arisen, involving new, low-mass physics, below the GeV scale, with extremely weak interaction strength, to address long-standing questions.  In light of theoretical predictions for particles like dark matter, the possibility of feebly interacting particles is emerging, even hinted at in current data.  A thriving, theoretically grounded experimental search for such particles is now underway, led by the success of the LHC, aiming to identify new physics within the Standard Model's boundaries.  Here we describe these efforts and objectives with a special emphasis on research involving particle accelerators and experiments that will be instrumental in finding feebly interacting particles.  These objectives are set against timeframes from short-term projects to long-term facilities spanning several decades.  These goals are articulated within the context of overarching questions and related sub-questions.  A review is also provided on current progress and prospects for future developments. Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating the migration dynamics through the naming game with migrating entities reveals how migration affects language development. (i) In scenarios where all agents are mobile, a collective phenomenon emerges that promotes language homogenization. This effect is highly consistent and observable across various agent densities and mobility levels. (ii) However, when only multi-lingual individuals are allowed to move, monolingual groups often form. Surprisingly, a sufficiently high mobility rate can lead to the spontaneous formation of a common language. This process occurs through a dynamic interaction between migrating groups, causing monolingual islands to break apart and merge into larger, bilingual entities that eventually coalesce into a single, uniform language. Notably, a critical threshold exists, beyond which language development typically emerges. Furthermore, a proposed analytical model accurately captures this process, revealing that larger, homogeneous groups are more likely to emerge in scenarios where there's a surplus of bilingual individuals within a mobile, multi-lingual population. These findings not only validate existing theories on language development but also shed new light on the complex and multifaceted nature of language evolution. They further compare and contrast the naming game with simulations of language development and the emergence of lingua-franca. Ultimately, these results provide valuable insights for understanding language development in real-world scenarios.
