Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), offers a novel solution. This supervised neural network technique is designed for real-time, variable analysis across complete temporal sequences, utilizing a low-dimensional representation of trend patterns. By incorporating trend patterns as features instead of individual variables, SGTM-TT overcomes the issue of variable independence and avoids the problem of redundant variables. Furthermore, its probabilistic mapping allows it to tackle missing data and variable importance effectively. We demonstrate that SGTM-TT's ability to identify relevant variables is significantly better than existing approaches and provides more accurate predictions. Notably, this is evident in matrix comparison across different dimensions, as well as when incorporating new batch data into the model. Our results show that SGTM-TT outperforms Supervised Principal Component Regression (PCReg) in variable identification and achieves first-step prediction accuracy on unexplored batch data. Finally, our proposed approach facilitates the analysis of complex microarray data used in expression learning. By incorporating learning profiles instead of variable-dependent properties, SGTM-Tt produces a low-dimensional representation of trend patterns, which are challenging to find in complex data. We successfully identify and extract trend patterns from a gene expression data set used in differentiating a variety of classes. Our results show that SGTM-Tt outperforms PCReg in variable identification and provides more accurate one-step ahead predictions. Overall, our approach provides a novel solution to the problem of variable analysis across complete temporal sequences and real-time prediction. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, traditional temporal difference learning algorithms are often paired with recurrent neural networks to approximate these valuations. We propose a new research, which separates the valuation function into two parts: one predicting the reward stream and another predicting the transition probabilities, achieving better results by combining these components with a dual-stochastic gradient method. Experimental validation shows that the proposed approach leads to higher returns and stabilizes the training process by reducing the estimation burden on the recurrent neural network and revealing the inner dynamics of the state space. We further leverage this separation to create a dual policy, which contributes to higher returns by differentiating control actions from state transitions. Finally, we explore the possibility of one agent learning these components separately and transferring them to others through inter-task data matching, resulting in better outcomes. The proposed ideas are demonstrated to be compatible with existing off-policy algorithms and open-source data to support reproducibility. Experimental results show promising improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in tasks such as Atari games, the grid world, and Mattar-like experiments. Moreover, an evaluation of the transition value function shows that the underlying dynamics of the learned states can be better reconstructed, leading to reduced estimation complexity during state representation learning. As a result, a large portion of detection accuracy is lost when actions are divided into frames or clips.  This paper introduces an innovative approach by integrating single-frame, clip-level, and action boundary constraints to enhance detection accuracy. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards. Moreover, we found that using REC plus moderate filtering yields similar model accuracy to a leading differential privacy method, at a substantial reduction in communication costs. Our code is available on a publicly accessible repository. Additionally, we have developed a novel tool for analyzing communication costs, which provides model-agnostic analysis and can be found at a specified repository URL. This tool allows for a comprehensive evaluation of these costs across various compression algorithms. In particular, we observed that using relative entropy coding in the training of a BERT language model results in significant communication savings, and our tool provides an efficient method for model quantization. Furthermore, we have developed a tool called PyDPG, which automatically generates deployment guides for models that utilize differential privacy and provides advice on how to effectively deploy these models while maintaining data privacy. One of the key contributions of this research is the identification of specific parameter values that maximize communication efficiency while meeting differential privacy requirements. To facilitate these optimizations, we have developed a dynamic programming-based algorithm, which provides an efficient solution to the complex problem of optimizing communication costs while ensuring differential privacy. We have evaluated our approach on a variety of datasets, compressors, and differential privacy mechanisms, and found that a specific configuration of this algorithm results in an average compression factor of 32 for the ShuffileNet model when trained on the CIFAR10 dataset, at a fixed differential privacy setting. By leveraging our tool, PyDPG-guided, which provides guidance on how to effectively deploy private models, we found that it yields a better user experience in terms of latency and power consumption. Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches based on publicly available data. One such method, recently proposed, leverages open-source geotagged Twitter posts to derive population counts for specified regions. By applying a Bayesian latent variable model to integrate diverse data sources, this approach achieves a more comprehensive view of the population. By focusing on the distribution of Twitter posts rather than individual users, it can accurately represent populations with varying degrees of coverage, heterogeneity, and heteroscedasticity. Moreover, this methodology enables the calculation of reliable population estimates based solely on the available data, thus avoiding the need for prior assumptions. Experiments conducted within the United States have demonstrated the efficacy of this approach by producing parameter estimates that align with the results of traditional census methods. The details of this research are documented at https://populationfromtwitter.github.io/. We are currently exploring similar approaches using data from Instagram and other social media platforms to expand the scope of this technique. The underlying code is open-source and available at https://github.com/ populationfromtwitter/PopulationFromTwitter. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. We also investigated the effects of light-based association and spin-exchange collisions acting simultaneously, leading to an emergent multi-particle atom-molecule condensation when dark-state conditions are met. Furthermore, we explored an alternative approach to coherent atom-molecule conversion using a beam that induces association, and demonstrated the emergence of a molecular condensate with oscillating population. Finally, we considered an optimized light pulse scheme to produce a massive number of bosonic spin units via coherent atom-molecule conversion, and found that the emergence of a macroscopic molecule condstate is feasible despite finite spin-exchange collision rates. In all the analyzed cases, the coherent atom-molecule conversion was shown to be insensitive to relevant light parameters, and thus could be effectively controlled using coherent optical techniques. The presented ideas, if implemented, offer an innovative and highly controllable method to produce massive numbers of spinless bosons, as well as coherent atom-molecule pairs, and can be considered a significant advancement in the field of quantum gas research. The proposed methods may also contribute to the development of innovative quantum information processing tools, and aid in overcoming current limitations associated with spin-exchange collisions, including the impossibility of producing a macroscopic number of spin units in Bose-Einstein condensates, and the difficulty in converting a Bose-Einstein condensate into another Bose-Einstein condensate with a different spin unit number. The presented ideas essentially allow the coherent atom-molecule conversion to overcome these limitations.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. This achievement marks the first demonstration of a versatile, data-driven application on a quantum computer, paving the way for handling massive datasets with significant reductions in computation time. Moreover, we estimate that our algorithm could successfully process datasets with millions of data points and thousands of dimensions within seconds, an estimated 100-150 times faster than classical hardware. This study also addresses the fragility of near-term quantum computing by using an adaptive noise reduction technique to minimize errors through continuous measurement. Consequently, our algorithm is suitable for near-term quantum devices, offering an important step towards a quantum learning ecosystem. It is available for download at [github.com/QuantumCEBQL/cebql](github.com/ibName/cebql). We anticipate that our code will facilitate the adoption of quantum computing by machine learning researchers, thereby promoting applications that leverage this innovative technology. This work is further described in [arXiv:2106.05163](arxiv.org/abs/arXiv:2106.05163). To promote a community-driven development of quantum computing and machine learning, we invite machine learning researchers to try their hand at implementing quantum applications, encouraging an exchange of ideas and knowledge that leads to breakthroughs. A tutorial illustrating the use of quantum tools for developing and simulating quantum applications, including classification and clustering, can be found at [quantum-ml-tutorial.github.io](quantum-ml-tutorial.github.io). In the future, we anticipate that quantum reinforcement learning will reveal novel applications that leverage the strengths of both technologies, an area we have explored in a related study, [arXiv:2103.13418](arxiv.org/abs/arXiv:2103.13418]. A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average value.  In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice characteristics, which helps make new speech samples sound more similar to existing ones.  We also developed a training technique where FastPitch is taught to change pitch in a way that makes natural speech patterns, and then we combined this with a neural network that can change pitch.  The results show that using these algorithms makes FastPitch easier to control, and synthesis quality gets better too.  In particular, tests on the LJSpeech dataset showed significant improvements in speech quality when using our algorithms, while also making it faster to control pitch, better able to handle big changes in pitch, and more generally, better able to change pitch.  The algorithms can also be used to improve a similar TTS model called Tacotron, which we did by coming up with new data for it to train on. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal reasoning problems within visual data by developing an end-to-end modular framework incorporating memory mechanisms to retain temporary object state awareness and relational information between objects in a video. A novel approach, the Object Presence Module, detects when temporary objects in a video appear or disappear, enabling the identification of their states. A second module, the Relational Position Module, documents the positional interactions among temporary objects, combining this information with the basic features of a video to generate multiple alternative outcomes via a modular attention mechanism. Experimentation on the CATER dataset, which tests temporary object state awareness and relational information, shows our method achieves the highest accuracy in all benchmarks, while evaluations on video question answering datasets show our method surpasses or matches state-of-the-art performance. Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study uses long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared gas
disk, and the results reveal a link between the planets' relative sizes and the
formation of gaps in the disk. However, when both planets form simultaneously,
their masses converge to a narrow range over a relatively short period of time.
Delaying one planet's development slightly increases their size disparity but
ultimately yields a similar mass ratio. To replicate observed exoplanet mass
variations, models suggest planets form and grow at different times and then
either disperse quickly from the gas disk or have gas supply interrupted early. 
Planets developing after others tend to have lower masses due to reduced gas
availability. However, a secondary gas accretion phase is critical in determining
giant planet mass ratios, as systems with a low mass ratio require a later gas
intake for the smaller planet. To reproduce various planetary mass ratios, a
range of scenarios emerge as possible: discoveries of numerous, short-lived planets
in hot Jupiter populations suggesting early gas dispersion, evidence for a delay
in giant planet formation for Earth-like planets, implications of delayed gas
accretion affecting super-Earth mass variations, and detection of many, low-mass
planets indicating early gas disk clearance. These results imply that a universal
planetary formation sequence does not exist. Instead, diverse planetary mass ratios
arising from variations in gas availability over various planetary development
timescales could explain the observed exoplanet patterns. Moreover, discrete
planetary formation groups might be linked to distinct periods in gas disk
evolution and/or changes in formation location or density. To fully grasp the
formation of planetary systems and their characteristics, it is essential to
consider their underlying architecture and evolutionary history. By analyzing the
planetary mass distribution, we can infer details about the disk's dynamics and
evolution, ultimately offering significant insights into planetary formation. 
As more precise exoplanet masses become available, we may uncover additional
trends in the planetary mass distribution, which could be interpreted within the
framework of planetary formation theory, thereby shedding light on the
complexity of planetary assembly and its intricate links with the surrounding

The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two distinct entropy terms. The first term optimizes cluster compactness by maximizing inter-cluster separation and minimizing within-cluster variance. The second term dynamically weights features according to their unique contributions, promoting better data partitioning. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through multiple datasets and comparisons with established state-of-the-art clustering methods. The results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed algorithm in achieving high-quality clusters with improved accuracy, specificity, and diversity compared to alternative clustering techniques. Moreover, we apply our algorithm to a real-world bioinformatics problem - protein structure prediction, showcasing its potential applications and outstanding performance on the benchmark ASN1 dataset. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. This new algorithm uniquely estimates expert parameters through an analysis of weight differential distributions, providing standalone solutions for both expert and weight optimization. As a result, it is compatible with any expert type, including traditional recurrent neural networks and modern transformer architectures, making it a highly versatile tool. Extensive experiments confirm that this new algorithm consistently converges to optimal solutions across a variety of scenarios, a capability confirmed both theoretically and through empirical testing. Additionally, the paper showcases the first successful applications of MoE models for long-form video comprehension and integrating MoE into the popular Transformer architecture. The new algorithm's implementation is freely available at github.com/moensk/moe-td. Overall, this paper provides an in-depth analysis of MoE model challenges, proposes a groundbreaking algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of tasks, and successfully applies this new approach to the challenging tasks of long-form video comprehension and transformer ensemble learning. Unlike traditional algorithms, this new approach does not depend on tasks, differentiable activation functions, and is compatible with any expert type, making it a fundamental contribution to the MoE learning community. Our results confirm that this new approach consistently outperforms traditional algorithms, both on their parameter configurations of their own and our proposed method, underscoring its superiority. Our analysis reveals that this new approach consistently learns parameter configurations significantly different from those obtained with traditional algorithms, a capability confirmed both theoretically and through empirical testing. Our data shows that this new approach consistently outperforms previous algorithms, both on their own parameter settings and our proposed method, with results indicating that our approach consistently achieves better performance. The new algorithm's fundamental contributions include its compatibility with any expert type, differentiable activation functions, and non-differentiable expert modes, making it a foundational piece of the MoE learning community. To further facilitate the continuation of MoE learning research, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of its applications, successfully applying the new approach to the challenging tasks of long-form video comprehension and transformer ensemble learning. Overall, the new algorithm presented in this paper constitutes a groundbreaking contribution to the MoE learning community

A continuous phase shift for the graviton is represented by a spinor $\eta$ that undergoes a self-adaptive transformation when coupled with twisted higher-spin fields.  A spinor in the left-moving sector of $AdS_3$ gravity is proposed that acts as a carrier for the graviton's continuous phase shift.  A two-dimensional graviton wavefunction in terms of the spinor $\eta$ is formulated.  A wavefunction for two-dimensional gravitons is formulated in the context of a Torus three-geometric partition function, a representation of three-geometric cosmology. Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the FUV fluxes with theoretical models, including those for blue horizontal branch and blue straggler stars, utilizing data from Gaia's BP/RP photometry. Out of 2325 source FUV-to-UV color ratios were calculated and analyzed in terms of their physical properties. Furthermore, the correlations between FUV flux, temperature, and metallicity were established through a binary star analysis, revealing temperatures between 10400K and 12500K and a wide range of metallicity, from -0.71 to +0.32 times the solar metallicity. The most prominent characteristic of NGC 4147's blue horizontal branch stars (BHB) is their distinctively low FUV-to-UV ratio when compared to blue straggler stars (BSS), with a significantly wider temperature range for the BHB stars. An enhanced presence of BSS near the core of NGC 4147 was also detected, which can be attributed to a specific dynamic process termed 'blue enrichment'. Our analysis further suggests a relatively young age for NGC 4147, around 7.4 billion years, based on a range of parameters including a distance of 10.5 kpc, a solary mass of 0.15 times the solar mass, a pre-main-sequence mass of 0.8 times the solar mass, a core radius of 4.46 pc, a half-radius of 16.22 pc, a total luminosity of 3.6 times 10^3 L and a central brightness of 4.6 magnitudes. A significant number of BSS in NGC 4147, around 25%, show temperatures above 10300K, indicating a subset of young stars known as the extreme blue stragglers, based on a range of theoretical models. An enhanced presence of these young E-BSS stars near the core of NGC 4147, around 15% and within 10 pc from the core, was also detected, which can be attributed to a specific dynamic process termed 'common envelope jets formation'. Furthermore, the parameters for NGC 4147, including its core radius, half-radius, and total luminosity, were found to be consistent with the overall globular cluster properties. Our analysis further reveals a range of photometric parameters for NGC 4147

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Additionally, it offers a more straightforward proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which relies on the fundamental theorem of tautological systems, a concept developed by Miller and Morita. Finally, this note proposes an extension of the b-principle to surface homeomorphisms, which would yield an approach to proving the asymptotic Madsen-Weiss theorem, but acknowledges that this particular problem may require alternative methods. It suggests that utilizing partial corectification could be a useful strategy for solving the asymptotic Madsen-Weiss theorem, and identifies oriented colored broken submersions as the most basic type of map functions that would benefit from the b-principle. (Note: This work was completed before the publication of Baldi and Behrens' related research, which reaches a similar conclusion using an alternative method.)

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called fine-tuning. There have been two commonly observed patterns of the relationship between model complexity and transferability: a correlation in smaller-scale models and opposition in larger-scale models. Furthermore, the issue of easy over-reliance might also contribute to decreased transferability. This study aims to investigate this relationship by focusing on one aspect: how often pre-trained DNNs rely on past experiences rather than developing new skills on downstream tasks. By using benchmarks such as ImageNet, we have created a unique set of modified benchmarks by incorporating new classes. The findings reveal that the relationship between model complexity and ease of over-reliance is U-shaped, indicating a significant and intricate connection. This discovery suggests that medium-complexity models are the most adaptable and able to effectively transfer knowledge. We have also identified that limiting a DNN's ability to easily draw from past experiences through data masking and noise injection can in fact boost transferability. Overall, the research provides valuable insights into the behavior of pre-trained DNNs and contributes to the development of more effective transfer learning methods. We have made the corresponding code available. This study offers practical advice for selecting the optimal size of the pre-trained model for specific downstream tasks as well as designing task datasets to boost the initial performance of the model. Furthermore, the findings indicate a new understanding of how easy reliance impacts transferability and set the stage for exploring other factors such as the impact of diverse training data on transfer learning in the future. As such, the research has the potential to drive the development of more human-like transferability capabilities for DNNs. We propose a novel approach to transfer learning that focuses on promoting deeper and more complex understanding of the downstream task in order to facilitate easier and more reliable transfer of knowledge from pre-trained models. By analyzing the key characteristics of pre-trained models that are essential for task success, we have identified new patterns and insights into how these characteristics evolve during the refinement process. We conclude by outlining a framework that aims to achieve a more human-like transfer learning capability by combining insights from cognitive science with developments in transfer learning theory and practice. In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics across multiple contexts, few have scrutinized the impact of network structure on information propagation efficiency. Our research applies the linear threshold model to networks comprised of communities, revealing that a network's information diffusion efficiency is closely linked to its modularity. Specifically, we derive two regimes: low modularity and high modularity scenarios. In low modularity scenarios, the key factors include the size of the largest community, the average cascade size, and the number of small communities. In high modularity scenarios, the diffusion efficiency is heavily influenced by the distribution of message reception probabilities across communities. Our findings are validated through a numerical approach based on a genetic algorithm. These insights are essential for designing targeted information dissemination strategies, particularly those involving communities, to minimize costs and increase effectiveness. Furthermore, our research offers practical recommendations for optimizing information spread in both network-based and time-based systems. In network-based systems, the use of high-reception-probability nodes as key information spreaders is proposed, while in time-based systems, the prioritization of early diffusion in key time periods is suggested. These guidelines can be used to improve the efficiency of information spread in both types of systems. Additionally, our research yields new performance metrics for the linear threshold model that are particularly useful for systems requiring spread optimization. If a spread is deemed unnecessary, the use of 'anti-influencers' with low reception probabilities can be proposed; if a spread is still viable with high reception probabilities, the distribution of reception probabilities across communities can be optimized. Our numerical simulations examine the impact of various network characteristics, such as size, degree distribution, and number of communities, to provide valuable guidelines. Furthermore, our research finds that even in systems with spread barriers, the presence of high reception probabilities is still crucial and can be identified through a new metric. These guidelines can be used in various scenarios across multiple fields. For instance, advertising targeting strategies can be developed by leveraging the structure of key social groups, pandemic mitigation plans can be designed by identifying the most effective spreading nodes and critical dissemination periods, and targeted advertising systems can be constructed by leveraging the structure of key social groups. Our research contributes a new method for designing optimal information spread in both network-based and time-based systems. Our research also provides generalizations to other models, such as the threshold model with delays and the independent cascade model. Our simulations examine the impact of high-reception-probability nodes

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, where malicious actors modify APK files directly to evade detection. The study aims to explore this type of attack that often receives insufficient attention due to a lack of knowledge or consideration of its potential consequences. We will examine the various forms of problem-space evasion attacks found in existing literature, such as source-level, intermediate-level, and problem-space-level attacks. We will also discuss the common evasion methods used, like code injection, grammatical alteration, neutralization, and neutralizing attacks. Furthermore, the study will discuss the shared characteristics of Android malware that complicates their detection using feature extraction methods. We will also discuss the most effective feature extraction techniques available and conclude by exploring and recommending future research avenues on this topic. This study is the first to comprehensive analyze the threat landscape of problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices in detail. The review of relevant literature related to this topic has been carried out in accordance with the standards of similar studies in this field. We have applied the PRISME framework for conducting the systematic literature review and gathered specific quantitative and qualitative data through a codebook to collect information from 28 included studies in this field. The main goal of this study is to contribute to the development of a research roadmap for protecting Android devices from problem-space evasion attacks by highlighting effective techniques, common attacks, and the shared characteristics of Android malware. The review of literature has been conducted in accordance with the relevant standards in this field. The study employs a novel framework known as REFRAME for organizing the analysis of literature related to this topic and collecting data using a codebook. We have thoroughly analyzed the common characteristics of Android malware that pose challenges to their detection using different feature extraction methods in this field. The study is targeted towards future researchers, developers, and practitioners who work in the area of problem-space evasion attacks and aims to contribute a comprehensive analysis of this topic for protecting Android devices. The review of literature has been conducted in a way that aligns with the standards of similar studies in this field and we believe that the analysis of various aspects of problem-space evasion attacks is a crucial step towards developing a research roadmap for protecting Android devices. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. The traditional perception of a service as self-contained software unit that exposes its functionality through clearly defined interface has given way to a more recent understanding: a service is any computable function with defined input and output formats. This distinction has significant implications, particularly in how services are secured. Traditional security approaches rely on verifying a service's interface through code inspection, but fail to account for potential internal vulnerabilities that could be exploited by an intermediary. In contrast, verifying a service's interface is insufficient for detecting vulnerabilities in intermediary services. To address these shortcomings, this research proposes securing services not through static interface verification, but rather by utilizing dynamic proof mechanisms that test a service's interface in real-time, including the use of QRCAs that incorporate rational inductive logic to define input/output formats. This novel approach is grounded in the understanding of composite services, where multiple services are concatenated in specific orders to achieve desired outcomes. An example use case illustrating the benefits of this security approach is also described, focusing on protecting consumer services from attacks originating on peer services. This research demonstrates that rational QRCAs enable robust and efficient security proof mechanisms for services, thereby preventing various types of attacks. Ultimately, the verification of services through rational QRCAs holds great potential for enhancing their security and trustworthiness. This study showcases the potential for model-based approaches to play a crucial role in verifying the behavior of software systems, thereby preventing adverse events. Furthermore, the integration of concepts from different semantic frameworks appears to pose fewer challenges than previously anticipated. On a more speculative note, this research raises intriguing questions about the role of concepts and ontologies in shaping applications and systems, thereby highlighting their potential for driving innovation and discovery. As the software industry looks to the future, the fundamental ideas explored in this study will hold significant relevance and continue to influence the evolution of the field. On a more speculative note, the journey described in the introduction involved several detours and changes in direction, with each development bringing us closer to our current understanding. This research tells the story of how our journey began with the simple discovery of service vulnerabilities, evolved into exploring new security approaches, and culminated in the development of concepts and ontologies as a means of mitigating these threats. Unlike other known phases such as Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, and PH-Pf phases, this new phase emerges at an intermediate mixing of Landau levels.  A proposed wave function accurately represents the unique topological structure of this phase by exhibiting high overlap with the exact ground state and closely reproducing the low-lying entanglement spectra, with topological characteristics that are resistant to flux changes.  Flux fluctuations also affect the pairing field in both phases, however, distinct behavior of the pairing field in the newly proposed phase has an unusual relationship with Landau level mixing, which is different from both the Pfaffian and PH-Pf phases, and transforms from s-wave to p-wave at a specific level of mixing.  Moreover, two types of gapless modes, consisting of edge counter-current Green's functions, develop in both phases along with a reoccurring edge mode that affects the Hall conductivity even in the gapped state.  A Hall conductivity of e^2/h, predicted for both phases, is consistent with the presence of this reoccurring edge mode, which also dictates thermal Hall conductivity in the insulating phase due to its dissipationless nature.  A Hall conductivity of e^2/h, predicted for both phases, is consistent with the presence of this reoccurring edge mode, which also contributes to thermal Hall conductivity in the insulating phase due to its dissipationless nature.  A distinction between the two phases, established through thermal Hall conductivity, which differs by a factor of 4 in both phases, was also identified.  A detailed comparison of the proposed wave function's overlap with numerical calculations in InAs quantum wells revealed that the pairing correlations exhibit an unusual level of nonlocality, which is significantly higher than local momenta correlations, in the insulating phase.  A distinction between single-particle and pair density correlations, which are both topologically stable, in the presence of flux changes, was also identified.  A detailed analysis of the proposed model's asymmetry as a function of Landau level mixing in both phases revealed that the pairing field's asymptotic behavior dominates the correlation gap at zero Landau level filling in the insulating phase.  A distinction between single-particle and pair density correlations, which are both topologically stable, in the presence of flux changes, was also identified.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve a single black hole feeding on non-interacting isotropic dust throughout the entire universe. This process results in a black hole forming from pure dust, a phenomenon that contradicts established notions. Meanwhile, investigating the membrane model of the universe, originally proposed by Wheeler, has shown that three distinct metric types can be created using a configuration involving three black holes embedded in a expanding universe space-time. However, the Thakurtra metric does not align with this space-time description. Moreover, examining the null energy condition has shown that the Thakurta metric does not exhibit negative energy; thus, the metric cannot be interpreted as a black hole within the membrane model of the universe. In addition, studies have shown that the Thakurta metric does not correspond to the expected properties of an event horizon either in a Schwarzschild or membrane model context. These findings indicate that the research by Böhm et al. was misinterpreted as it failed to identify the metric as a Thakurta black hole, and the metric does not exhibit negative energy; further, it does not align with either the Schwarzschild or membrane model of the universe. This has led to questions regarding whether the Thakurta metric can accurately model a black hole, and it necessitates the implementation of a different creation mechanism that will not involve unphysical processes in order to resolve the issues at hand. Further studies have shown that the issues can be resolved if one uses a creation mechanism involving a particle pair produced through quantum effects within a Schwarzschild space-time, a phenomenon occurring outside the event horizon, and the resulting particle pair can then give rise to a spherical shell space-time, a negative mass object forming between the two particles, and subsequently one of these particles can then give birth to a Thakurta black hole. This new description then enables one to calculate a proper color fluid stress-energy tensor. Furthermore, it has been shown that the issues can also be resolved if one views the Thakurta metric as a quasireversable description of a Schwarzschild space-time, a phenomenon that results from a reflection of the Schwarzschild space-time, including its matter content, through a two-dimensional cutting plane that is moving at the speed of light, a process that is theoretically supported by a well-known paper written by Ellis and Scarron; in this case, the metric can then be viewed as carrying a physical meaning

We ran simulations incorporating a global disc model with a Gaussian pressure profile and perturbations resembling wave patterns to mimic the effects of gas density fluctuations, allowing us to model planetary core formation at both pressure minima and maxima. We found that within the global disc model, the saddle point between inner and outer disc regions is particularly conducive to planet core formation. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our study indicates that this is indeed the case. We demonstrate specific learning tasks for which learners with computational limitations need significantly more parameters than those with theoretical upper bounds. Moreover, our results suggest that robust learning could necessitate even more parameters. Building upon a recent discovery, we further prove that bounded learners might need an exponentially greater number of parameters under robust conditions. To contrast our findings, we prove that bounded learners need only marginally more parameters in non-robust settings. Our study also implies that an approach that solely enhances a learner's computational capabilities could lead to the need for an exponentially greater number of parameters in robust conditions, while having little to no effect in non-robust conditions. We also present an algorithmic method to devise learning algorithms from programmable learners. Our study highlights the significance of computational constraints of the learner in understanding the need for overparameterization. Our results are based on the assumption that the target distribution contains noise, which is a widespread assumption in machine learning theory. Our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between computational and statistical limitations of the learner and the need for massive models. Our study sets a new theoretical boundary for the need for overparameterization in robust conditions, which could be further reduced through more efficient computational design. Our method also offers a novel way to develop learning algorithms from programmable learners and could be applied to different types of learners. Our study also demonstrates that our approach can facilitate a systematic evaluation of the need for overparameterization in a wide variety of machine learning tasks and datasets. Our results imply that an approach that solely enhances a learner's computational capabilities could lead to improved robustness, which is an important area of research. Our study highlights the significance of developing more effective learning algorithms that minimize the need for massive models and might inspire new machine learning architectures and techniques. Our findings also suggest that an exponential increase in the number of parameters required for robust conditions could be detrimental to real-world applications, which might necessitate further research into better design strategies. This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We conducted an extensive computational analysis involving up to 120 customers and ten vehicles, revealing that our method consistently outperforms a traditional mixed-integer programming formulation by finding significantly more optimal solutions and improved objective function values. Specifically, we observed a fourfold increase in optimal solution counts and up to a 4.7% reduction in objective function values compared to the baseline. Most optimality gaps closed for smaller instances (under 50 customers), while a 0.23% optimality gap remained for the largest instance (120 customers). We attribute this performance improvement to a 95.8% optimality rate for all instances and a 99.8% optimality rate for the medium and large instances, respectively. Notably, our results demonstrate that most non-optimal solutions shared a common characteristic: a pre-feasible path involving a direct connection between the departure and arrival times, though this path did not align with the optimal route. Consequently, introducing a valid inequality eliminating all pre-feasible paths with this characteristic characteristic led to a direct reduction in the optimality gap. We established a connection between the valid inequality and a well-known property of the shortest path in a graph, thus ensuring the validity of this inequality. This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system to enable a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients. Consequently, a comprehensive dataset containing images of different White Blood Cell types was used to evaluate and validate the effectiveness of various composite models, with the goal of identifying the best approach for use in future clinical practice. Furthermore, a system was designed and tested for classification purposes, with the results demonstrating the superiority of certain composite models over standalone deep neural networks and other classification techniques in terms of accuracy. Specifically, combining 3D Recurrent Neural Networks with 2D Convolutional Neural Networks achieved an impressive 93% cross validation accuracy, outperforming other composite models and individual deep neural networks. By utilizing composite models, it is possible to mitigate the limitations associated with deep neural networks for the analysis of structural information in medical imaging, resulting in significant advancements in accuracy. Therefore, these composite models provide a promising approach for use in various medical imaging applications where conventional deep neural networks fall short.

A recent approach resolves this issue by approximating the gauge potential using a reduced, subspace model of the Hamiltonian's matrix elements. We demonstrate this method's potential in optimizing the coherent generation of entangled microwave photons using a nonlinear LC circuit within the superconducting quantum circuit model. A four-photon state of specific symmetry can be efficiently produced, outperforming a strategy that involves rapid, discrete switches. Our results indicate the effectiveness and viability of the subspace model in practical quantum circuit applications. Additionally, the produced entangled photons exhibit non-classical properties, which are verified through direct measurement of the photon correlations. Furthermore, the impact of realistic noise sources on the performance accuracy is examined. With the increasing availability of powerful simulation tools, such as quantum processors and algorithms, this approach becomes more accessible than ever before. We've created a state-of-the-art laser-plasma platform to study fundamental photon-photon collision phenomena, such as the linear Breit-Wheeler process using real photons, by leveraging the Gemini laser facility at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory. The platform employs a high-powered laser wakefield accelerator and a bremsstrahlung converter to generate high-energy photon beams colliding with kiloelectronvolt x-ray photons emitted by a plasma target. The resulting Breit-Wheeler spectra were measured by an advanced pixel detector. Utilizing experimental data and simulations, we determined that with the current setup, a Breit-Wheeler signal has been detected equivalent to about 5% of the bremsstrahlung background radiation. To improve the signal-over-background ratio, we propose enhancements to the experiment. Firstly, we suggest using the laser to post-ionize the plasma target after its initial radiation, amplifying the bremsstrahlung signal. Secondly, we plan to increase the photon beam's polarization purity and ensure a more controlled collision geometry. According to simulations, these modifications will enhance the signal-over-background ratio to a level where polarisation-correlated Breit-Wheeler measurements can be accurately taken. Furthermore, we will be able to explore other photon-photon collision phenomena, such as the non-linear Breit-Wheeler process using electron-positron pair photons, by leveraging the enhanced Breit-Wheeler platform. The successful implementation of these improvements will represent a significant breakthrough in laboratory Breit-Wheeler measurements and serve as a cornerstone for investigating a range of multi-photon processes and testing quantum electrodynamics under extreme field conditions. Furthermore, we will be one step closer to developing powerful X-ray sources based on the Breit-Wheeler process. We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'key-covered', a determinable property that ensures consistency. Furthermore, we found this condition necessary and sufficient for a specific subset of weakly-recursive Shape Expression constraints to have universal solutions. We also investigated two specific data exchange scenarios: one where the target dependency has universal solutions, and another specific class of Shape Expression constraints. In the context of these settings, we successfully formulated corresponding data exchange problems as equivalent to well-known relational data exchange problems, thus providing a comprehensive solution. To accomplish this, we first converted the target dependencies into First-Order Logic, then applied established data exchange results via typed guarded first-order logic translations. Finally, we leveraged established results on typed guarded first-order logic to evaluate the feasibility of solutions, decidability of finite domain satisfaction, and the complexity of checking universal solutions for key-covered settings. Throughout our research, we recognized that certain data exchange problems may require infinite relational representations, a challenge that necessitated the development of new techniques to handle infinite expansions, particularly with typed IRI constructors that facilitate the creation of RDF IRIs from relational values and the translation of Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics and machine learning. Recent advancements in this field have significantly improved our understanding of productivity and efficiency analysis through techniques such as nonparametric frontier models. The application of novel regression methods in this context has crucial implications for monetary and trade policies. This paper provides a thorough overview of shape-constrained nonparametric regression, covering recent developments and future research avenues in the field. The review delves into nonparametric frontier models, focusing on classical and Bayesian approaches and examining the existing literature on vertical efficiency and efficiency determinants. Furthermore, we highlight significant advancements in recent literature, before highlighting intriguing challenges that still require full attention from the research community. The final section presents perspectives on promising avenues for future research in this field. This study proposes an innovative mass reconstruction technique for examining the LHC's same-sign W boson and same-sign Z boson production with low-mass scalars. Our approach can also detect non-resonant scenarios and provides feasible mass resolution enhancements. The analysis reveals that our method yields a mass resolution better than 5 GeV for same-sign Drell-Yan processes at the LHC's design luminosity, offering a parameter space detection limit below 10^3 pb for the same-sign W boson scenario. The low-mass Z boson search sets a detection limit of around 3.5 (4.5) fb at a mass range of 50 (60) GeV, all within a mass uncertainty of 10 GeV. The research further demonstrates that our technique can supplement existing searches, providing a mass reconstruction mechanism for beyond the Standard Model searches where the parent particle has a low mass. The findings highlight the feasibility of same-sign production for low-mass scalar characterization at the LHC. The projected mass resolution exhibits a linear improvement in inverse proportion to the luminosity achieved, that is, better luminosity leads to mass determination being better. The proposed mass reconstruction techniques represent a significant advancement and open up new possibilities for investigating beyond the Standard Model scenarios at the LHC. In particular, the low-mass Z boson analysis can be used to investigate the dark sector and establish a detection limit on the dark photon for masses between 60 and 400 GeV, assuming a dark photon to Z boson branching ratio of 1. The analysis can also be extended to other dark sectors by adjusting the branching ratio. The research shows that low-mass scalar production offers a unique opportunity to explore the low mass range of the Standard Model Higgs boson through a four-W boson channel, providing a mass determination of 60 GeV with a mass uncertainty of 9.6 GeV at the LHC's design luminosity. The analysis can be used to investigate beyond the Standard Model scenarios at the HL-LHC by conducting same-sign W and Z boson production searches at the mass range of the Higgs boson. The projected mass resolution for different luminosities shows that the mass determination improves at higher luminosity. The research shows that low-mass scalar production can be used to search for the mass range of the massless singlet scalar in the context of the simple mirror twin Higgs model. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand, making it challenging to fix errors or improve their capabilities without resetting their training. Explaining their behavior is particularly crucial in critical areas like medical imaging, where securing trust and collaboration from healthcare professionals is vital. A reliable explanation system would enable healthcare professionals to rely on model predictions, engage in meaningful discussions with researchers, and guide patients in a more informed manner. Nevertheless, existing explanation systems often provide superficial or irrelevant information, fueling skepticism rather than addressing it. In order to rectify this issue, a more systematic approach is needed to evaluate and enhance explanation systems. Towards this goal, we introduce a new methodology for evaluating the trustworthiness of image classification explanations provided by neural network-based interpreters. Using this method, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of eight different interpreters and found them to be untrustworthy, as they either failed to provide coherent explanations or were unable to do so effectively. Furthermore, we developed a new model that leverages BERT and attention-based mechanisms to deliver reliable and coherent explanations in the form of natural language, and demonstrated its superiority over current state-of-the-art models through various evaluation metrics and human assessments. By developing and testing this model, we aim to provide a more accurate understanding of how reliable deep neural network-based classifiers are, and what their limitations are, in the context of image classification. The code and data associated with this research are publicly available. Please note that the research was focused on image classification, and the methods and explanations discussed can be applied across different domains. However, the analysis and findings are specifically relevant to image classification. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from Z for free fermions to Z2 for interacting fermions. We also observed correlation's impact on the topological edge state of a 2D lattice. Additionally, we investigated the correlations in a 2D lattice and discovered that the system remains topological even under strong correlation. Our research on a 3D lattice shows that the impact of correlations in three-dimensional non-Hermitian systems is even more complex, with potential reference points serving as potential milestones for discovering new topological characteristics. We hope that the clear definitions of topological classification and cataloged systems in one-dimensional systems will guide future research, while the discovery of new topological characteristics in three-dimensional systems will stimulate extensive investigation. The present research is expected to contribute significantly to our comprehension of non-Hermitian topology by examining the interactions, thereby broadening the applicability of this research field. We release a correlation matrix-based classification scheme as supplementary information. We believe that the study of non-Hermitian topology can be leveraged to explore various experimental platforms, including photonic, phononic, and cold atoms, and that the discovery of novel topological characteristics will facilitate innovative applications. The present research is expected to facilitate future investigations into topological systems with interactions, and we release a correlation matrix-based classification scheme as supplementary information. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications; (ii) an economical use of model parameters and (iii) an efficient arrangement of keywords to minimize input dimensions, where each keyword is represented by a sequence rather than a static image. Our experiments on the Google Speech Command dataset demonstrate that CNN can identify keywords promptly, accurately detects them in less than 0.1s, and operates efficiently with only 0.11 million parameters. This model outperforms others in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Our NN-based system is more resilient to noise and more sensitive to audio content than traditional statistical-based systems, offering an enhanced alternative. The compact CNN is applicable to context recognition as well, employing a more efficient activation function to reduce context size. Our NN-based context recognition approach surpasses statistical methods and offers a practical solution for smart speaker context recognition. To promote user privacy, we integrated a user authentication feature into our system, employing the NN-based similarity measure to identify legitimate users, where the CNN is also applied to authenticate users efficiently. Our goal is to provide private, context-aware smart speaker functionality, encompassing user authentication and identification, keyword spotting, and context recognition; thus, we propose a system that integrates all three components. Our system has a significant advantage over the state-of-the-art method "Deep Scoring" in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, where the system has been successfully tested on the Google Speech dataset. A video demonstration of the system is available at https://www.cse.msu.edu/~hongzhang/system.html. Essentially, our system can be viewed as a privacy-preserving smart speaker that integrates keyword spotting and context recognition, where user authentication and identification are also integrated into the system to facilitate user privacy. The system's components are interchangeable and can thus be used in any sequence. Our system has a key benefit over prior methods like "Deep Scoring" in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. A system demonstration video is accessible at https://www.cse.msu.edu/~hongzhang/system.html. The compact CNN was implemented using TensorFlow open-source platform; the platform can be accessed at https://github.com/google/tensorflow. A code snapshot of the system is available at https://www.cse.msu.edu/~hongzhang/systemcode.html.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, however, are designed with the lens orientation perpendicular to the direction of gravity. Failing to consider this aspect may lead to inaccurate stitching of images. To develop accurate stitching, considering the alignment of images captured with devices oriented perpendicular to gravity is necessary. To address this issue, researchers proposed a method for calculating the angle of rotation, based on the presence of a straight horizontal line in the captured image. To determine this angle, a camera is simulated as looking at a flat screen from a distance. By using a straight line on the screen as the point of intersection on the circle, the camera's rotation is calculated as being perpendicular to this line. To determine the point of intersection, a linear equation representing the screen's straight line is derived based on the captured image. By simulating the captured image as a projection of the captured scene, the point of intersection on the circle is determined. Researchers derived an analytical expression for calculating the angle of rotation, based on the captured image, in addition to designing an algorithm for implementing this expression in a program. Testing the expression's effectiveness using images captured with devices oriented perpendicularly to gravity showed a 95% match with simulated camera orientations, a 90% match with device orientations, and a 85% match with images in the wild. Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, we develop a random tensor network model that calculates long-time behavior of entanglement entropy and reflected entropy within a random quantum circuit.  We identify a transition phase in the entropy metrics that indicates a significant shift in their growth rates.  By using an approximate method to correct this shift, we derive a theoretical model that can be compared with the random tensor network results.  Moreover, the model explains a notable phenomenon observed in the network output - a sudden increase in reflected entropy relative to entanglement entropy during the Page transition phase.  This increase indicates a positive information carrying capacity between the system and the environmental subsystems within the entanglement wedge.  Instead of the expected entanglement monotonic growth, we discover a specific environment influenced variation where the reflected entropy surpasses it.  Ultimately, the model attributes this phenomenon to a residual nonlocality effect stemming from the tensor network's direct evaluation method.  Further refinement of the network's evaluation method should eliminate this residual effect, thereby reducing the reflected entropy relative to the entanglement entropy throughout the transition phase.  Consequently, the model's findings offer a theoretical basis for improving the network's representation of entanglement structure and thus a more accurate understanding of the nonlocality phenomenon.  Furthermore, the model's generalizability to other cross-sectional areas asymmetries is also explored.  Lastly, the model's implications for the random tensor network representation accuracy are discussed in relation to specific information theory metrics.  It is hypothesized that the tensor network model can be further refined by improving its representation of a specific entropy metric - the triangular entropy - which is expected to yield a more accurate reflection of the entanglement structure across the transition phase.  To verify this hypothesis, we derive an analytical expression of the triangular entropy using holographic theory and compare it to the random tensor network model.  Ultimately, the model reveals two primary shortcomings of the network model that may be responsible for the residual effect - its incomplete sampling of certain network configurations and an inadequate randomization method.  By addressing these shortcomings, we develop a binary tree network model that can generate the same entropy metrics as the random tensor network and thus a more accurate understanding of the entanglement structure.  Consequently, the model's generalizability to other physics phenomena that share similar structure and symmetry characteristics is also explored.  In conclusion, the analysis delves into the potential limitations of the tensor network

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock registers two tunneling times,  $\tau_y$ and $\tau_z$, corresponding to particles approaching a potential barrier in the $y$ or $z$ direction. There is a discrepancy between the definition of tunneling time by B{\"u}ttiker and Steinberg, with the latter identifying the actual tunneling time (ATT) with the Larmor clock reading for the $y$ direction. Research, however, has shown that ATT is influenced by spin fluctuations in non-commuting spin systems. Consequently, we've established an ATT based on fluctuations that is given by the expression $\tau_y + \frac{\tau_z^2}{\tau_y}$. This new definition is applicable across various situations and is consistent with recent experiments. Additionally, we've performed a comprehensive review of recent studies on tunneling time and found that most previous attempts failed to account for spin fluctuations. They often resulted in unrealistic or failing definitions of ATT. In contrast, our proposed framework offers a coherent and consistent approach based on a physical model. With the emergence of quantum computing and new advances in quantum matter, accurately measuring tunneling time has become increasingly important. The distinction between ATT and classical time can help determine when quantum effects will prevail. For example, in quantum computing candidate MoSe$_2$, we've found that ATT is much shorter than classical time, indicating that quantum contact may not be feasible even at a distance of one Bohr radius. This finding presents an obstacle that must be overcome for quantum computing using monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides. While recent studies have failed to achieve quantum computing candidate status for these materials, they have successfully designed topological insulators and non-linear optics within them. In summary, we've demonstrated that measuring tunneling time has far-reaching implications for both fundamental research and applications in condensed matter physics, highlights the importance of correctly defining tunneling time, and opens a new field for exploring tunneling time in transition metal dichalcogenides. Furthermore, we've identified a new paradigm for studying tunneling time using Larmor precession in a weak magnetic field as a universal and powerful tool. The simplicity of this setup has the potential to revolutionize condensed matter photonics by measuring ATT, detecting spin fluctuations and exploring new physical properties. This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function common to all mesons of the same parity but differing flavor. Specifically for the B meson, we utilize the QCD sum rules to establish the normalization constant and the leading moment of the amplitude, while acknowledging the need for further research to determine the leading twist distribution function in P-wave non-relativistic mesons, crucial for constructing an accurate anomalous dimension matrix for the leading twist amplitudes. We explore the role of the universal function in determining the shape of the leading twist amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, examining how it influences the production properties of P-wave non-relativistic B mesons. Our research also includes an analysis of the double moments of the amplitudes, essential for analyzing exclusive processes involving P-wave non-relativistic mesons, such as decays and form factors. This capability will enable us to predict values including the ratio of the decay rate to the leading twist contribution in the calculation, all for P-wave non-relativistic B mesons. Additionally, we utilize the QCD sum rules with theads of heavy mesons, including charm and bottom types, to establish the normalization constant and the leading moment of the amplitude for the charged pseudoscalar decay of a heavy to a lighter meson, while discussing its applicability and limitations. We explore the role of the sum rules in this analysis, while acknowledging the need for further research in this area. Moreover, we utilize the QCD sum rules with a light quark to establish the normalization constant and the leading moment of the amplitude for the decay of a light to a lighter vector meson, while discussing its features and limitations. We predict values including the ratio of the decay rate to the leading twist contribution in the calculation, essential for understanding the process. This research provides an in-depth analysis of the leading twist distribution amplitudes in P-wave non-relativistic mesons under non-relativistic QCD framework and the light cone QCD sum rules approach, while highlighting several open questions for future study. By combining NRQCD and QCD sum rules, we have a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of amplitudes at a different energy scale compared to the standard sum rules approach, but this research shows that both frameworks share a significant quantity - the universal function, signifying a significant symmetry in these amplitudes. Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. The task becomes particularly demanding when models need to learn online after seeing each example only once. Current techniques often struggle to adapt or come with restrictions like non-transparency and the inability to learn in an online fashion. To overcome this issue, we introduce an innovative approach called OCEAN, an online continual learning method for classification problems. OCEAN involves creating a memory bank of class centroids, dynamically updating it after each example, and assigning each data point to the nearest centroid. The differences between assignments and current centroids then form features for a model that predicts data point assignments. The proposed model is differentiable and can be optimized end-to-end using an ensemble loss function. This loss function, derived from an analysis of the assignment vector properties, is simple, adaptable, and comes without any hyperparameters. The experimental results show that OCEAN outperforms established online and incremental learning methods, performing almost as well as models trained in a non-incremental, non-online manner on benchmark datasets. The proposed approach offers an online, incremental, and transparent solution for classification tasks. The code for this approach can be found at https://github.com/quantvast/Ocean. The research reveals a surprising insight: simple yet well-designed ensemble loss can effectively tackle the core challenges of continual learning. The proposed model, along with the findings, can be utilized to improve incremental and online learning algorithms for classification tasks. In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve applying Cartan's structure equations and generalizing them to explore new concepts. By associating flat generalized connections with a metric, researchers gain new insights into Einstein's vacuum equations and their solutions in four-dimensional Lorentzian geometry. This work showcases how particular generalized connections and geometries can effectively encode Ricci flat metrics in unique and novel ways. Furthermore, it demonstrates that certain generalized flat geometries are linked to classical Einstein's vacuum solutions, and finally, it poses open questions regarding the inverse problem, asking if a generalized metric can be recovered from a given Einstein's vacuum solution. By expanding the search for new metrics in general relativity, this work aims to inspire innovative geometries and theories in metric geometry and general relations. The connection to local calculations, generalized flat geometries, and Einstein's equations suggests a substantial inverse problem, requiring an in-depth investigation. In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$. Moreover, we establish a generalization of both the permutation equivalents of the Chow-Laigwizd and the Permu-Tezcan results, using a generalized approach. At its core, our method involves employing linear combinations of monic, low-degree polynomials to obtain new polynomial sets, one of which remains monic after linear combination. After employing resultant elimination methods to obtain new polynomial sets, our primary task becomes an equation-solving exercise in multivariate fields. Following this, we use the properties of $q$-th roots in multivariate fields to isolate the coefficients of our constructed polynomials as elements of subfields, with cube orders, which in turn allows us to establish the required permutation polynomial criteria.
