To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping Majorana-related conductance oscillations with those controlled by the sample temperature. We developed an alternative tunneling theory, taking into account a widely varying distribution of tunneling strengths. This leads to the appearance of Majorana peaks in tunneling conductance as the temperature drops. In the standard Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer channel, the distribution of tunneling strengths is governed by a Gaussian random variable. We employed numerical simulations to investigate a log-normal distribution, which was also analytically analyzed. We discovered that in both cases, the tunneling conductance displays non-oscillating behavior at high temperatures, whereas at lower temperatures, it begins oscillating at a specific temperature that is proportional to log-normal tunneling strength. We suggest that majorana conductance peaks should show a significant change as the temperature drops, in contrast to non-majorana peaks. This distinction allows us to focus on majorana physics and eliminate standard tunneling effects by performing experiments at varying temperatures and analyzing majorana conductance peaks in the resulting temperature-dependent trends. We found that majorana conductance peaks should be highly sensitive, significantly decreasing even at relatively low temperatures, while the critical temperature at which they appear is remarkably consistent across different majorana sizes. Furthermore, majorana conductance peaks should either not be present or only appear weakly at very low temperatures, indicating a significant change in their behavior. We found that majorana conductance peaks should either not be present or only appear strongly at very low temperatures, significantly decreasing above a certain temperature threshold. We calculated this critical temperature and found that majorana conductance peaks should either not be present or only appear strongly below 1.5 K, 2 K, and 2.5 K for majorana sizes of 90%, 93%, and 95%, respectively. Consequently, our method involves combining temperature-dependent tunneling statistics with majorana physics to investigate the distinct nature of majorana conductance peaks. We propose an experiment that integrates a sample with varying temperatures and analyzes majorana conductance peaks in the resulting temperature-dependent trends. This will allow us to distinguish between majorana and non-majorana peaks, achieve majorana conductance peaks that are highly sensitive, significantly decreasing even at relatively low temperatures, which is highly desirable. The performance of linear bandit algorithms can be evaluated by considering their approximation power, determined by the eigenvalues of their design matrices. However, when dealing with action spaces that exhibit structural properties, the eigenvalues-based approximation power measure does not accurately reflect the true approximation capabilities. In such cases, we utilize the spectral norm to establish a more suitable approximation power measure. Building on this, we present a universal threshold for linear bandit regimes with structured action spaces, which can be linearly searched. This allows us to develop a "one-size-fits-all" bandit algorithm with nearly optimal regret for a broad range of these structures. Additionally, we illustrate the effectiveness of this algorithm in scenarios with unstructured action spaces, achieving a regret that scales logarithmically with d. This is in contrast to the known upper bound of O(\sqrt{d}) that has been established for such cases in prior work. All algorithmic developments, including the bandit algorithms, are implemented at a statistical testbench, which can be publicly accessed. This includes the universal threshold for general action spaces, determined through numerical computations. Furthermore, we present numerical results demonstrating the effectiveness of our algorithm designed for structured action spaces, even when applied to unstructured action spaces, and show that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in many scenarios. The design matrices used in these computations were generated at a publicly accessible GitHub repository. In general, the proposed bandit algorithms achieved significantly better cumulative regret compared to the competing algorithms, across various action space dimensions and regimes. In particular, for action spaces with a dimension d greater than or equal to 1000, our algorithm exhibited a significantly lower regret, amounting to at least two orders of magnitude, in comparison to the regret obtained with the best alternative approach. The proposed universal threshold for general action spaces, determined through numerical computations, showed a nearly exact match with the expected eigenvalues-based spectral approximation power measure, as determined using the computationally efficient Estimation of Spectral Eigenvalue Density (ESED) tool. In other words, the spectral norm-based measure held little additional value in this case, as the expected eigenvalues-based measure already accurately reflected the true approximation power. In contrast, for action spaces with a dimension d less than 10, the spectral norm-based measure exceeded the expected eigenvalues-based measure, indicating that the expected eigenvalues-based measure does not accurately reflect the true approximation power in this case. In general, the expected eigenvalues-based spectral approximation power measure has been found to accurately reflect the true approximation power for action spaces

differences. Including magnitude data helps mitigate these issues, but in some 
situations covering magnitudes from other bands may not be effective. 
We've developed a novel method utilizing a density-based approach with the 
integration of photometric information. By employing color-magnitude diagrams 
to determine pairwise relationships, we successfully identify potential associations 
despite large spatial discrepancies. Experimental results demonstrate the method 
outperforms existing methods using only spatial data and highlights the benefits 
of incorporating photometric information to estimate stellar properties. 
This approach can be applied generally to match photometric catalogs containing 
magnitude information, including those derived from spectroscopic or time-
variable data. To facilitate wider utilization, we've released the system as an 
open-source software tool, applicable across diverse photometric catalogs. 
The source code is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/chpmvr/pipeline. 
A pre-built executable version is available for download at https://nstar.cpt.nthu.edu.tw/.

further optimize this matching process and reduce errors. As the software is

testing and development.

data analysis tasks.

software. 
Ultimately, our long-term goal is to make the system a cloud-based service, 
accessible via a web interface for easy application and integration into various 
photometric catalogs. 
In addition to catalog matching, we've identified potential areas of improvement 
for correcting photometric calibration issues and activating the system as a 
powerful tool for spectroscopic analysis.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. Furthermore, experts suggested numerous opportunities for further improvement and indicated a desire to see OntoPlot integrated with Protégé. As a result, we propose Protégé-OntoPlot, a groundbreaking hybrid visualisation system, marking the first collaborative effort to integrate an standalone visualisation tool with an industry-leading ontology editor. This integration has the potential to substantially improve domain experts' experience, enabling them to focus on higher-level tasks and leveraging both OntoPlot's visualisation capabilities and Protégé's comprehensive editing features. With OntoPlot's user study indicating a considerable decrease in visualisation errors, we expect the Protégé-OntoPlot hybrid to lead to substantial quality improvements in ontology editing. Additionally, we anticipate that OntoPlot's hybrid visualisation strategy can be successfully applied to other complex knowledge graphs, enhancing understanding and reducing visual clutter. The proposed hybrid is poised to significantly enhance the efficient visualisation of knowledge graphs in general. Based on these findings and the considerable interest exhibited by domain experts, we firmly believe that OntoPlot has the potential to become an indispensable tool for domain specialists and knowledge engineers. Furthermore, we expect the Protégé-OntoPlot integration to become a significant breakthrough, enabling a substantial improvement in domain experts' experience and ontology quality. To achieve this vision, we plan to continue refining and optimise the Protégé-OntoPlot integration, paving the way for its adoption in various ontology editing and visualisation tasks. By making Protégé-OntoPlot available to the public, we aim to accelerate the advancement of ontology engineering and contribute to a substantial quality improvement in ontology editing. When the release point is set early, the irregularity becomes apparent around the midpoint of the throw; however, a delayed release point yields mid-air corrections that obscure the irregularity until the ball enters its final phase, necessitating observers to rely on earlier, less detailed visual cues to detect the irregularity. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' fundamental theorem shows that if a function f(n) approaches infinity as n increases, then the limit of ex(n, F) over n squared approaches f(n) times pi(F) as n approaches infinity. We show that the Turan number ex(n, F) of an 3-uniform graph F, which is the disjoint union of two complete graphs with an edge, is equal to n squared minus n with probability approaching one as n increases. We prove this by analyzing a random graph and using a central binomial distribution limit theorem. We also use an integer division property of n to bound ex(n, F) from below by showing it is greater than half n squared minus n with probability approaching one as n increases, assuming a condition on n that has density one as n increases. We use an induction on the maximum Turan number graph F' such that F is a subset of F', starting from Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem, to prove the inequality. We also prove a conjecture of Baber and Talbot that the limit of ex(n, F) over n squared is equal to n times a rational number as n increases for certain graphs F that have an induced cycle. We prove this by using a method to bound the maximum Turan number of an n vertex graph that has an induced cycle, which bounds ex(n, F) from above and below. We also prove a conjecture of Gao that the limit of ex(n, F) over n squared as n increases is equal to n times zero point seven three nine times n times a rational number as n increases for a graph F that has an induced cycle. We prove this by using the results from the previous conjecture and the fact that the limit of ex(n, F) over n squared is equal to zero if and only if the limit of ex(n, F') over n squared is equal to zero for all induced subgraphs F' of F as n increases. We also give conjectures on the real number that the limit of ex(n, F) over n squared approaches as n increases for certain graphs

To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the required amount of labeled images. Focusing on detecting pneumonia, we evaluate the efficiency of various image improvement strategies - including division by gamma, inversion, adding noise, perturbing, rotating, translating, and combining these methods - within two distinct deep learning architectures: UNet and efficient UNet. By utilizing only 100 trained images, we assess the segmentation accuracy in detecting pneumonia on unseen images from the RSNA Pneumonia Detection Challenge dataset after applying various image enhancement strategies. Ultimately, we discover that utilizing only 100 trained images after combining gamma inversion and perturbation along with training data directly results in the highest validation AUPRC of 0.9162, thus significantly decreasing the necessity for labeled data. Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and allows for the adaptation of captions based on their intended style. We achieve this by incorporating a flexible prompt system that incorporates lexical and semantic hints. This prompt system is trained end-to-end using a combined objective function, which is composed of a weighted sum of cross-entropy losses and a masked language loss. Furthermore, to broaden the model's ability to process diverse semantic hints, we incorporate an external knowledge source in the form of concept graphs. By doing this, we are able to expand the vocabulary of concept tokens, which enhances the semantic scope of the prompts and, by extension, the captions. Experimental evaluations conducted on the COCO-2014 and Concept12 datasets confirm that our proposed model outperforms the current state-of-the-art image captioning models. Additionally, we are able to successfully classify the desired style of an image caption based on its prompt, outperforming the best previously-used classification model in this capacity. This paper presents an innovative image captioning framework that is versatile, adaptable, and efficient. For a detailed discussion of the code used to support this research, see https://github.com/guoxg1219/ flexible-image-captioning. This code was developed using an end-to-end training approach, which is also described in the research. This approach is notable for the fact that the prompts used to guide the image captioning process are learned during training, much like how adaptive methods handle non-linear functions. This research further expands the use of flexible text generation models, which initially dealt primarily with tasks such as translation and summarization, into the domain of image captioning. Ultimately, we are able to successfully adapt our proposed framework to other computer vision tasks, which we believe will have a significant positive impact on future research in this area. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality research. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. The utility of the definition is further showcased through a regulatory analysis of an autonomous system example, revealing that current regulations lack clarity on causality and utility, particularly in complex cases. The paper suggests that causal-based definitions of harm and the proposed qualitative harm concept provide valuable tools for clarifying these ambiguities. By focusing on causality, the definition of qualitative harm may ultimately contribute to the development of more effective regulations for autonomous systems, thus minimizing legal uncertainty surrounding these systems and their societal integration. The integration of causal models and an emphasis on utility may also pave the way for using artificial intelligence tools, such as causal models, to facilitate decision-making regarding qualitative harm in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, the effectiveness of the proposed definition of qualitative harm will be evaluated through its ability to guide regulatory decisions regarding general settings of exceptions for autonomous systems. The incorporation of the definition's integration with decision-making tools containing causal models represents an essential step in the integration of autonomous systems into our society. The definition of qualitative harm may also serve as a valuable tool for evaluating cases of harm caused by the exploitation of personal data and the resulting loss of utility. In the context of data exploitation, the definition of qualitative harm may assist in specifying the types of harm that can be avoided, thereby highlighting the importance of providing protection for personal data. The discussion of how the definition of qualitative harm relates to various types of harm, such as qualitative harm, financial harm, emotional harm, and physical harm, also reveals its potential utility. The definition of qualitative harm may ultimately contribute to the development of more effective protection and compensation mechanisms for personal data, thus enhancing societal integration of autonomous systems. The proposed definition of qualitative harm may also facilitate public engagement and discourse on the complex topic of harm in autonomous systems, ultimately leading to a greater awareness of the need for regulation and the potential consequences of systems that have not been adequately regulated. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws. The speech-to-text process would be significantly simplified if, after recognizing speech, the system could directly translate the resulting phonetic representation, a capability known as zero-shot translation. This research introduces a new speech-to-text task that utilizes out-of-vocabulary speech tokens for translation, a feature not previously supported by existing machine translation datasets. This innovation gives rise to a new challenge: translating novel data points, a problem known as zero-shot translation. To address this challenge, we first create a dataset, SpeechTranslationSim, designed to mimic real-world speech-to-text translation tasks. This dataset consists of a speech corpus with annotated translation, a translation corpus with annotated speech, and a phonetic translation corpus with annotated phonetics. This dataset enables a direct comparison between different speech-to-text architectures, a feature previously absent from existing datasets. We then test an out-of-vocabulary speech-to-text model, an end-to-end system with out-of-vocabulary token IDs, on zero-shot and known-label translation tasks, comparing its performance to a baseline out-of-vocabulary speech-to-text model, an end-to-end system without out-of-vocabulary token IDs. The results show that adding out-of-vocabulary token IDs leads to mixed improvements in translation quality. To a limited extent, we observe better zero-shot translation performance with SpeechTranslationSim, a dataset that mimics real-world speech-to-text translation tasks. The use of token IDs, an out-of-vocabulary phonetic translator, appears to be a key factor. The SpeechTranslationSim dataset, an end-to-end system, and the out-of-vocabulary token ID model are available at the link: https://github.com/AyushaRajendran/SpeechTranslationSim. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain. These novel systems of heat conduction encompass and refine multiple existing models, including those due to Pillaria, Fabrizio and Pinnigetti, Farid and Ziadi, and Majda and McGilvery. Utilizing standard tools like the Galerkin method for spatial boundary regularization and the Moore-Penrose method for handling rank-deficient dissipation matrices, we establish the well-posedness of these novel models through direct approaches. This comprehensive study provides a thorough mathematical framework for a broad class of diffuse heat and mass flux boundary conditions, which can be optimized over time for a given initial-state realizations. Consequently, this novel framework might offer novel avenues for the numerical simulation of processes influenced by heat conduction, contact, mass transfer, elasticity, hydrodynamics, electromagnetism, and other interconnected physical phenomena. Furthermore, we analyze the long-term behavior of these models, evaluating the approaches to a steady-state solution. Specifically, we prove the existence of a steady-state solution for systems satisfying certain dissipation principles and provide explicit representations of coercivity for boundary memories using integral forms, which can be applied even when the boundary data have fading memory. To accommodate models without coercivity constraints, we incorporate cut-off techniques and establish growth conditions for the nonlinear terms in conjunction with dynamic boundary conditions. These novel extensions significantly broaden the applicability of existing methods to novel models of heat conduction, contact, mass transfer, and other interconnected physical phenomena. Furthermore, our models may find applications in other fields as well. As a particular case, we verify the well-posedness of a model due to Majda and McGilvery, which lacks coercivity constraints on the boundary. This novel extension might offer insights into the behavior of a diffuse mass transfer process at a boundary, such as the diffusion of gases from a solid surface. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods frequently struggle to characterize these spikes adequately. This issue highlights the need for an alternative approach combining probabilistic forecasts with peak demand predictions, which can provide more reliable estimates, particularly during peak hours and at lower network levels, leading to more effective load management and network planning decisions. We examined probabilistic forecasting performed separately on aggregated and disaggregated consumption, followed by peak demand estimation using classification techniques to enhance accuracy. This method yielded significant improvements in peak demand forecasting accuracy among a small customer population, with the peak hours exhibiting higher gains and non-peak hours also experiencing gains, although to a lesser extent. Crucially, the success of this strategy is contingent on accurate probabilistic consumption forecasting, which can be achieved with improved uncertainty assessment methods, particularly for highly disaggregated markets. By prioritizing peak demand estimation, we can minimize variability and capture the inherent characteristics of consumer behavior, which manifest differently during peak hours compared to non-peak hours within disaggregated consumption scenarios. This investigation marks one of the first forays into aggregating probabilistic consumption forecasts, which has the potential to revolutionize energy and mobility forecasting fields. In the context of this research, we analyzed data from a micro distribution network populated with approximately 600 customers to validate our findings and assess the impact of our proposed method on accuracy, which we measured using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) and the Graz Reliability System, which revealed a notable improvement in the forecast's capability to predict the distribution of peak demand among the studied population, with the peak hours experiencing a reduction in expected loss (ELOSS) of 11.66% and the non-peak hours seeing a decrease of 4.23%. In an effort to make the proposed approach more feasible for widespread adoption, we have created a advanced Web-based platform designed to assist network operators and researchers working with disaggregated energy datasets, which we have dubbed MultiScatter. By providing this platform within an internet browser environment, we can ensure seamless accessibility and facilitate the analysis of datasets populating with energy data, which we have demonstrated using the previously mentioned dataset as well as an additional 42kAG energy dataset, which accommodates approximately 42,000 customers and spans the period of 2020

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple possible ways to present the same information and the risk of misleading data. A structured approach to representation can mitigate these issues to some extent. Our paper focuses on the u-Net architecture, a prevalent model for medical image analysis that often incorporates additional knowledge. We examine the impact of three distinct methods integrating segmentation knowledge into a model, specifically semantic segmentation, multi-task learning, and pseudo-segmentation. We compare the efficacy of these methods on two datasets from the's says in Brain 2020 competition focused on fracture detection. Our experiments reveal that incorporating segmentation knowledge does not necessarily enhance model performance but can significantly impact the underlying training objectives. Based on these findings, we recommend a novel training approach that combines two objectives with pseudo-segmentation, resulting in superior performance compared to the top-ranking solution on the competition leaderboard. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/denisposluyeko/brain2020. Ultimately, we discovered that incorporating relevant information from multiple domains can be more effective in achieving high-quality machine learning outcomes. A accompanying neural network with mixed focus continues this research in a different direction. This new model is designed to learn the common features shared between two related tasks with a novel structure that differs from the standard multi-task learning architecture. The model's efficacy was tested by retraining u-Net on the Medico dataset focused on skin cancer identification, achieving a 4% increase in AUC score in comparison to the original model. Consequently, the paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of the effects of integrating knowledge from various sources in deep learning models with a specific application to the u-Net architecture for medical image analysis. Alongside presenting the study's findings, the paper aims to contribute a systematic approach to resolving the ongoing challenges in this field. Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings. To resolve these issues and minimize labeling expenses, we introduce an unsupervised anomaly-detection framework that uses deep learning methods. Our approach leverages two separate autoencoders, incorporating anomaly detection and normalization methods to mitigate data inconsistencies related to COVID-19 appearance. The proposed framework is applied to three public datasets to develop distinct classification systems, each of which achieves enhanced performance and reduced annotation requirements. Our test demonstrated that our approach can accurately identify COVID-19 infections on unlabelled scans while distinguishing between bacterial pneumonia and normal cases. The resulting outcomes demonstrate that our system outperforms previously proposed unsupervised anomaly detectors, with significant improvements in F1 scores and AUC metrics for the ALA and Normal/Bacterial classes, respectively. By incorporating an edge loss regularization technique, we were able to eliminate artificial boundaries and show that our approach leads to more accurate predictions on unlabelled cases. The findings suggest that the proposed unsupervised approach is effective for anomaly detection and classification on chest CT scans, with potential applications in practical applications. The project's source code is available for public review at the following link: https://github.com/fatimazardouiri/CovidCT UDAC. Our team also contributed to a related competitive data challenge, finishing in the top 3 out of 261 participating teams. Due to data privacy restrictions, the model has not been tested on real patient data; however, further evaluations are planned to ensure its generalizability on diverse clinical populations. The accurate positioning of vertebras in clinical settings is crucial for the diagnosis of various pathologies such as scoliosis, vertebral fractures, and spinal cord injuries. However, this task is challenging due to the limited visibility of vertebras in two-dimensional X-ray images. In this paper, a method is proposed to locate and count vertebras in X-ray images of the entire spine, focusing on simplifying the complex problem of vertebral identification. By introducing a set of predefined rules based on vertebral anatomy, the proposed approach is able to filter out unlikely vertebral identities in X-ray images and accurately deploy a model for the localization of vertebras. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 92.3% in the identification of vertebral identities and 88.3% in their corresponding counts. Notably, the proposed approach demonstrates the largest advantage over existing models in the localization of vertebras in difficult cases involving fractures or osteoporosis. When applied to the full spine, the proposed approach demonstrates the highest accuracy in the combined localization of vertebras compared to other approaches, while also showcasing significant gains in the localization of vertebras in individual segments. Specifically, the proposed approach achieves an accuracy of 85.9% in the localization of vertebras in full spine X-ray images, demonstrating the highest advantage over existing models in this context. Within a theoretical framework, this study examines the process of free electrons colliding with a multilevel, spatially-replicated polariton system. Prior to reaching thermal equilibrium, a typical multilevel transmitter is initially excited and undergos spontaneous emission, resulting in the creation of a multilevel, spatially-replicated polariton system, where each level corresponds to a different energy state. Meanwhile, a multilevel transmitter, which may also exhibit auto-resonance in this system, continues to emit polaritons as it tunnels past them due to a repulsive barrier. When an electron collides with a polariton and transfers its energy, a new polariton is formed, potentially triggering a tunnelling event for the next electron. This process forms the basis of a novel mechanism for non-electrical energy generation and conversion. Analytical predictions indicate that, under specific conditions, this system can generate energies of up to 1000 times the value of the energy generated by the polariton system when it first forms. Furthermore, this study also examines the possibility of electrical energy conversion via the repulsive barrier, giving rise to novel applications within photonics. Ultimately, two potential implementations are presented for the development of devices based on the polariton electron collider, namely an optical wavefront collimator and a photonically-controlled electron accelerator. These devices could potentially be constructed using a repulsive potential in optical emitters, such as GaN nanocolumns, and other materials. This study also proposes an innovative method for detecting and analysing the temporal properties of photons, which could be implemented using the optical properties of the GaN nanocolumns. This technique is capable of detecting and analysing the temporal properties of photons on a microsecond scale. Moreover, this study estimates the time required for the pumping of a multilevel transmitter to be around one hour at room temperature. Consequently, this study proposes that, in order to reduce the time required, a low temperature and high concentration plasma should be used to create the polariton electron collider. This study also presents an alternative design that combines the spatially-replicated polariton system with a quantum dot, which could reduce the time required for the pumping of a multilevel transmitter and improve the efficiency of energy conversion. Analytical predictions indicate that, under specific conditions, this alternative design can convert energies up to three orders of magnitude greater than those which match the energy generated by the polariton system when it first forms. Ultimately, this study presents an evaluation of the feasibility of the polariton

In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated by central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to rapidly develop an open-loop controller for the actual robot dynamics. Following that, we implement feedback controllers, starting with partial feedback inversion to guide the adaptation process, and then introducing feedback activation to enhance stability and efficiency. We successfully tested our novel, model-based feedback controller on the CheetaX4, a quadruped robot, and observed significant improvements in dynamics, energy efficiency, and overall performance. Comprehensive video documentation and an open-source software framework are available for replication and further improvement. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate a seamless transition of optimal controllers from simulation to real robots, potentially expanding to various robotic applications. We propose a variational quantum algorithm, referred to as the variational separability verifier (VSV), with the goal of identifying whether a given multi-qubit quantum state exhibits separable properties during execution. To achieve this, we develop a variational separation indicator that serves as a measure for determining separability, built upon the tensor-nuclear-decomposition approximation and optimized via an alternating least-squares variational-quantum algorithm. Our research utilizes VSV on simulations involving quantum states of up to $8$ qubits and demonstrates that, even with limited qubits and relatively low numbers of variational steps, this algorithm can effectively distinguish separable states while experiencing a notable decrease in fidelity as a result of noise and limited qubit counts. Furthermore, we investigate the indicator's behavior in cases involving entangled states, such as Bell states. Our VSV protocol may have implications for facilitating separability analysis, a crucial issue within various quantum information technologies.

A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes fine-scale magnetic reconnections and the formation of magnetic islands. Prior research suggested that these modes remain relatively slow-moving because of their small scales. However, theoretical predictions indicated a boundary beyond which these modes would transition into turbulent behavior. This study discovered that this threshold is not just a boundary, but rather a boundary of comprehensive plasma instability. Consequently, this analysis suggests that turbulent plasma behavior is inherent within magnetic reconnection processes that involve island formation, and this is not an exception but rather a universal rule. Moreover, this research proposes a new theory - the electron-temperature-triggered transition from quasi-coherent to turbulent behavior of magnetic reconnections. Experimental findings confirm that this transition is marked by a sharp decrease in the mode's wavelength and a corresponding shift in the energy spectrum's scaling ratio. This study was conducted using data obtained from the Gas Dynamic Chamber of the Binaural Spherical Probe during the Solar Probe Plus mission's Flight 1. An electrostatic mode was observed here for the first time. An analytical comparison with theoretical predictions yielded highly encouraging results, confirming that this experimental finding aligned almost exactly with the predicted transition theory. Consequently, this research identified a new type of plasma process - the electron-temperature-triggered transition from coherent to turbulent behavior of magnetic reconnections. This study also proposed a new theoretical framework - the electron-temperature-triggered transition from coherent to turbulent magnetic reconnections. This research also yielded several secondary findings and hypotheses. Firstly, this study proposed a new theoretical framework for the electron-temperature-triggered transition from coherent to turbulent magnetic reconnections. Secondly, this research revealed that this transition is characterized by a series of chain reactions. Thirdly, this study proposed a new theoretical framework for the energy spectrum's scaling ratio. Lastly, this research proposed a new hypothesis - the Solar Probe Plus mission's observations may lead to a groundbreaking new area in the exploration of the Solar Corona. A cutting-edge task called fashion attribute manipulation is becoming increasingly significant in image editing applications. Our research introduces ComPaX, the largest and most accurate database for this task, which enables reliable image manipulation and attribution. In comparison to existing datasets, ComPaX substantially enhances the number of possible attribute modifications and accuracy of its labeling system. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process intricate and labor-intensive. This paper proposes a straightforward and efficient cost constructor based on codewords, yielding a $O(N)$ complexity compared to the conventional $O(N^2)$ complexity. Our constructor is versatile, one-size-fits-all, and is effectively integrated into the existing low-dimensional light field depth estimation networks, thereby improving the estimation precision. We demonstrate that incorporating our constructor into the DCW-LFNet, PDW-LFNet, and JW-LFNet can significantly enhance their performance by 0.32, 0.25, and 0.20 dB respectively.
